name: feedback_aggregate_crosstab_required_for_causal_claims
description: "Separate aggregate breakdowns (e.g. entitlement status, activity status, outcome buckets) can't be combined into a causal/predictive claim or used to justify prioritizing one group without an account-level cross-tab"
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: feedback
  originSessionId: b1dcbd23-de1b-44b1-a6a0-82d2269ebbf8
  modified: 2026-09-20T13:03:01.068Z
---

When a draft has multiple independent aggregate counts over the same account population (e.g. renewal-month buckets, entitlement status, active-work status), each is only a marginal distribution. Without an account-level cross-tab, you cannot infer how they relate to each other, and you cannot use one breakdown to justify prioritizing a group defined by a *different* breakdown.

**Why:** Surfaced 2027-09-24 reviewing a CS draft that claimed "active Customer Success work predicts renewal" and used that to recommend prioritizing the 154 active-entitlement accounts — but active CS work only covered 49 accounts, entitlement status is an unrelated variable, and there was no renewal outcome data at all (only renewal month, which is scheduling, not result). Two distinct errors compounded: a causal/predictive claim asserted with zero outcome data, and a recommendation that silently swapped in the wrong population.

**How to apply:** When reviewing evidence drafts (CS, Growth, or similar), check (1) whether an outcome variable actually exists before allowing predictive/causal language, and (2) whether the population named in the recommendation matches the population the claim was actually made about. If either check fails, report the breakdowns as separate descriptive counts and strip the causal/predictive language. Same family as [[feedback_expansion_assist_eligibility_vs_exposure]] (don't blend distinct status counts into one funnel number) and [[feedback_workaround_vs_institutional_evidence]] (don't let one type of evidence stand in for a different claim).

name: feedback_beta_chart_framing
description: "Beta support-load charts should show per-account distribution and category mix, not just totals, and must not editorialize into an access-widening recommendation"
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: feedback
  originSessionId: 45d28ee0-1205-4265-a968-d9fd9f3b978a
  modified: 2026-09-12T22:06:17.412Z
---

For beta support-question charts: show support questions per active beta account, the category mix, and whether questions are concentrated in a few accounts (i.e. distribution, not just a total count).

**Why:** user explicitly does not want a handful of difficult/high-volume accounts read as evidence the whole beta is struggling, and does not want the chart itself to carry or imply a recommendation to widen access — that's a separate decision, not something a support-load chart should push toward. Consistent with how prior beta issues were kept scoped and non-escalatory ([[project_admin_role_permission_confusion]], [[project_helio_start_retry_tile_artifact]]).

**How to apply:** when building/updating beta-related charts (Helio Start or future betas), default to per-account breakdowns and concentration views over aggregate totals, and keep any narrative/annotation descriptive (what's happening) rather than prescriptive (what to do about access/scope).

name: feedback_cs_auto_nudge_zero_errors_wording
description: "Don't summarize CS auto-nudge (or similar) evidence-consistency results as \"zero decision errors\" — state the specific evidence instead"
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: feedback
  originSessionId: cb60546d-32f1-4932-a4fe-d80f5777619b
  modified: 2026-09-18T23:04:27.758Z
---

When summarizing evidence from the CS auto-nudge review (or similar governed-field consistency checks, see [[project_cs_auto_nudge_operating_review_may8_jun13_2025]]), do not compress the result into a phrase like "zero decision errors."

State the underlying evidence directly instead: no evaluated decision carried a different governed-field status across the corresponding reporting and lifecycle views, and no customer correction was required.

Also hold the standing definition precisely: external-system authority means verified readiness to perform the connector's required owner-level permission or network-allowlist action. It is not permission for automated contact.

**Why:** "zero decision errors" overclaims — it implies a broader error-free guarantee than what was actually checked (cross-view field-status consistency, not correctness of every decision made). This is consistent with the user's standing pattern of avoiding early/overclaiming framing (see [[feedback_interim_maturity_no_early_call]], [[feedback_quarter_close_no_victory_lap_framing]]).

**How to apply:** in any final-language or executive-facing pass on this review or similar governed-field consistency evidence, use the precise evidence statement above rather than a summary claim of zero errors, and keep the external-system-authority definition scoped to connector readiness, never outreach/contact consent.

name: feedback-cs-launch-handoff-card-coverage-wording
description: Helio Start CS launch handoff card must not claim 24/7 coverage or immediate after-hours response
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: feedback
  originSessionId: 494cedb5-fd55-4330-80db-631fcffa9ead
  modified: 2026-09-20T14:08:02.548Z
---

Corrected 2027-10-30: a Helio Start CS launch handoff card stated "Helio Start paid traffic has 24/7 live Customer Success coverage. After-hours cases are handled immediately by the backup." This overstates the approved coverage on two counts: (1) the staffed window is Monday-Friday 8:00am-6:00pm Central, not 24/7; (2) the named backup takes an after-hours case at the next service opening, not immediately. Account-level support minutes running continuously from first contact is a separate fact (about the support-minute clock, not staffing hours) and should not be blended into a claim of round-the-clock live coverage.

**Why:** Matches the standing staffing design in [[project_cs_owner_permission_handoff_design_draft_aug2027]] (Mon-Fri 8am-6pm CT, backup queues to next opening, uninterrupted support-minute clock) and the same overclaim pattern flagged in [[feedback_helio_checklist_tracking_heading_framing]] — don't let a continuity/measurement fact get restated as a staffing-hours or response-speed claim.

**How to apply:** When reviewing any Helio Start CS-facing or launch-facing copy (handoff cards, checklists, training material), state coverage as Mon-Fri 8am-6pm CT staffed, after-hours cases queued to next service opening, and account-level support minutes continuous from first contact — as three distinct facts, never collapsed into "24/7" or "immediate."

name: feedback-cs-training-no-queued-reminder-wording
description: CS support-training copy must not describe held/stale-setup records as a queue that auto-sends once data catches up
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: feedback
  originSessionId: 2fff95bd-e2ea-4078-bdc0-505dad00f412
  modified: 2026-09-20T13:53:37.597Z
---

Corrected 2027-10-22: a CS support-training draft stated "Records with missing or stale setup data are queued for reminder delivery. Once the data catches up, the reminder is sent automatically." This is wrong on two counts: (1) a held record is not sitting in a queue waiting for delivery — there is no queue/write-back mechanism; (2) there is no "automatic" send once data catches up — every possible display/decision requires a fresh evaluation of the source fields at that moment, not a resumption of a previously queued action.

**Why:** Matches the standing display-only, no-write-back architecture in [[feedback_setup_readiness_summary_display_rules]] — the summary/state is recomputed from current source-field freshness each time, never persisted as a pending action waiting to fire. Describing it as a queue implies a write-back/auto-trigger path that doesn't exist and was explicitly ruled out.

**How to apply:** When reviewing CS-facing docs, training material, or copy about setup-readiness/held records, flag any language implying queuing, automatic resumption, or delayed-but-guaranteed delivery. Correct wording should state that each display/decision is freshly evaluated against current source-field state, not that a held record is "waiting" for the data to arrive.

name: feedback-stabilization-cohort
description: "Standing rule — first cohort to cross statistical significance doesn't ship; wait one more stabilization cohort week before rollout"
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: feedback
  originSessionId: d88e8f18-9f42-441e-b3f4-db66647d0d0a
  modified: 2026-09-20T04:59:25.944Z
---

When an experiment read first crosses statistical significance, don't ship/roll out on that read alone — wait one additional stabilization cohort week to confirm the effect holds, then ship.

**Why:** The user set this as an explicit standing rule as of 2023-03-26, prompted by EXP-2023-02-onboarding-trigger crossing significance (week-1 retention +2.9pts, p=0.05, n=220) right after the confound-tainted EXP-2023-02-pricing-page mess (see [[project_churn_cut_staff]]). The concern is "fake-first-significance" — a borderline result (p=0.05) that looks real the moment it crosses the threshold but regresses toward the mean with more data. This generalizes the user's established pattern throughout the churn investigation of not declaring results before they're solid (tier-split, denominator checks, activation-day confirmation, powered reads over early peeks).

**How to apply:** When any experiment first crosses significance, recommend against immediate rollout/shipping even if the result looks clean. Suggest waiting for one more cohort week to see the effect hold before treating it as a confirmed win. This applies generally to future experiments, not just EXP-2023-02-onboarding-trigger.

**Validated 2023-04-03:** the rule worked as intended on the case that created it — EXP-2023-02-onboarding-trigger's second cohort confirmed the first (pooled +3.1pts, p=0.04, n=420), and the user called it only after that second crossing, not on the first p=0.05 read (see [[project_churn_cut_staff]]). Keep applying this rule with confidence to future first-significance moments.

**Validated 2023-12-08, opposite direction:** the setup-reminder retention test (see [[project_setup_reminder_retention_test]]) crossed first significance at +0.7pts/p=.04, then its stabilization cohort came in at only +0.2pts/p=.31 — combined +0.4pts/p=.09, correctly recorded as inconclusive rather than shipped. This is the "fake-first-significance" failure mode the rule was originally designed to catch (see Why above), now demonstrated concretely rather than just theorized. The rule protects against false positives, not just confirms true ones.

**2024-01-11, practice landed beyond the user's own judgment:** the [[project_stabilization_training_exercise]] session ran with mixed Growth/CS groups — all 6 groups independently rewrote a first-significant result as not-ready-to-ship once walked through denominator/window/audience-risk gaps. The same day, a real CS renewal readout (owner distinct from the [[project_renewal_risk_pilot_lane]] Sept-cohort work — this one on collaborator-invite count, 260/312 classified, 83.1% vs 71.3%, +11.8pts) was independently revised by its own owner to lead with full denominator and effect size, flag 52 unclassified accounts and missing support/lifecycle-risk outcomes, and mark itself descriptive/not-ready-to-ship — without escalating to Owen or Ines as an approval gate. The rule is now operating as institutional practice, not just something the user personally enforces case by case.

**2024-03-13, sample audit confirms institutionalization at scale:** Owen and Ines audited 12 Growth/CS readouts produced since the January training and sent findings to Priya. 10 of 12 had denominator and effect size before the conclusion on first submission; 2 were self-corrected before any decision (one hidden incomplete observation window, one missing lifecycle audience-risk split). Of 3 readouts that hit first significance in the period, 1 later stabilized and shipped, 2 failed to reproduce and were correctly held rather than shipped — a second real-world confirmation of the "fake-first-significance" failure mode (see 2023-12-08 entry above). Teams are applying the practice without routing every decision back through the user, Owen, or Ines.

**2024-03-15, formalized as standing practice, deliberately not centralized:** at the beyond-Q1 decision meeting, the user and Priya closed out the Q1 audit decision by keeping this framework as the standing readout practice for Growth and CS (denominator/effect-size-first, stabilization wait, lifecycle-risk review). See [[project_investigation_framework_standing_practice]] for full detail. They explicitly declined to make it a companywide mandatory template or route readouts through the user/Owen/Ines as an approval gate — Owen owns the readout-shape standard, Ines owns the lifecycle-risk standard.

**2024-03-25, applied to Helio Start's first mature cohort:** Priya agreed with the user's denominator-first read on the first mature Helio Start cohort (67.6% activation, see [[project_helio_start_first_mature_cohort_read]]). Consistent with the rule, they did not treat the single cohort's 67.6% as a trend, did not broaden eligibility, and did not relax the routed-before-setup rules on the strength of one read — the next mature cohort will be judged on its own evidence before any of those calls are revisited.

**2027-07-06, Growth formalized a revised experiment method that codifies this rule:** primary metric and minimum detectable effect are declared before launch; the powered read runs a fixed 21 days; effect size and confidence interval are reported alongside the result; one scheduled interim review is allowed but is limited to safety guardrails only and cannot trigger rollout; a complete stabilization cohort is required before any ship decision. This is Growth's own pre-registration + fixed-duration-read formalization of the same "don't ship on first significance" principle above — apply it as the current standing method for Growth experiment reads going forward, and treat any interim-review result someone tries to use to justify shipping as out of bounds even if it looks favorable.

**Same day, method-only approval note issued:** reviewed against the full standing framework in [[project_investigation_framework_standing_practice]]. The revision fully covers the significance/read-window/stabilization mechanics (pre-registration, fixed 21-day read, interim safety-only, stabilization required before ship) but does not itself restate denominator-first reporting or the lifecycle audience-risk review (Ines-owned). Those two requirements were treated as still in force via existing practice, not superseded or newly waived by this document — future readouts under this method should still carry them. The approval note was scoped to the method only: no endorsement of any product hypothesis and no read of any specific experiment result.

**2027-07-22, first live application of the revised method under its one scheduled interim review:** a Growth experiment that began its predeclared 21-day fixed run on 2027-07-13 reached its single scheduled safety-only interim review on schedule. No predeclared safety guardrail crossed its stop condition. The declared primary metric, minimum detectable effect, powered window, and required stabilization cohort were all left unchanged. A favorable secondary completion measure showed up but was correctly kept exploratory rather than used to justify any rollout or product conclusion — consistent with the 2027-07-06 rule that interim-review results, even favorable ones, are out of bounds for shipping decisions. The run continues under the approved method; no ship/no-ship call is due until the fixed 21-day read completes and stabilization is confirmed.

**2027-08-10, final read + stabilization cohort complete — correctly held as inconclusive:** the same experiment's fixed 21-day powered window (2027-07-13 to 2027-08-02, n=24,860) closed with +0.6pp (95% CI +0.1 to +1.1) — CI excludes zero but the point estimate falls short of the predeclared +0.8pp minimum detectable effect. The required stabilization cohort (2027-08-03 to 2027-08-09, n=8,302) then came in at +0.4pp (95% CI -0.3 to +1.1), non-significant. No safety guardrail crossed in either window. This is a third real-world instance of the fake-first-significance pattern (see 2023-12-08 and 2024-03-13 entries above) and the first full end-to-end run under the 2027-07-06 formalized method — correctly read as inconclusive/not-ready-to-ship rather than a confirmed win, consistent with the rule holding even when the primary window nominally crosses significance.

Chosen over a 15.2¢/kWh variable plan, since actual usage (820-1,050 kWh) falls in the cheaper mid-to-high tier and the lease now covers the full plan term.

**Why:** With the lease term now locked in and exceeding the plan term, the early-termination risk that motivated the month-to-month bridge no longer applies, and the fixed rate beats the variable rate at the household's usage level.

Supplier confirmed in writing on 8-19-25 that the fixed plan became active on 8-13-25 (terms unchanged). Status is now active, not confirmation-pending — nothing remains outstanding on the switch.

First post-switch statement (billing period 7-22-25–8-21-25) confirmed the split billed correctly: 296 kWh on the prior variable plan through 8-12-25, 128 kWh on the fixed plan from 8-13-25, no recurring plan fee, no early-termination charge.

First full statement under the fixed plan (billing period ending ~9-25-25): 911 kWh, energy $109.32 + delivery $22.44 = $131.76 pre-tax (~14.5¢/kWh), $133.87 total with tax (~14.7¢/kWh) — no recurring plan fee, as expected. This is noticeably above the confirmed estimate: interpolating the quoted 14.1¢/kWh (500 kWh) / 13.5¢/kWh (1,000 kWh) tiers at 911 kWh predicts ~13.6¢/kWh, so actual billed rate ran roughly 6-7% higher than quoted.

On 8-13-26, the 8-13-25–8-12-26 fixed term ended and a new 12-month fixed plan took effect without interruption: 13.8¢/kWh flat (no tiered rate this time), no recurring plan fee, $150 early-termination charge, running 8-13-26 through 8-12-27. First statement under the new term expected ~9-3-26; user set a personal reminder for 9-3-26 7:00-7:10pm Central to verify the 13.8¢/kWh rate, no plan fee, and no erroneous transition charge.

**How to apply:** Prior monitoring concern (actual rate running ~6-7% above quoted estimate) applied to the now-expired term and its tiered-rate structure, which no longer applies under the flat 13.8¢/kWh renewal.

9-3-26 statement review (642 kWh, energy $88.60, plan fee $0.00, transition charge $0.00, taxes $2.11, total $90.71) confirms the billed rate matches the quoted flat 13.8¢/kWh exactly (642 × 0.138 = 88.596). name: project-cherrywood-water-usage-spike-investigation
description: "Cherrywood unit water usage spike Dec-Jan 2025 — CLOSED 4-4-25, full $42 credited, no household-leak finding"
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: project
  originSessionId: 3d16ae29-f9b4-4bae-a61d-268f73cbcf29
  modified: 2026-09-18T20:09:05.347Z
---

Cherrywood water usage jumped from 3,120 gallons (Dec 2024) to 6,480 gallons (Jan 2025) — more than double, with no rate change to explain it. Logged 2025-02-15.

In-unit checks all came back negative: no running toilet, no dripping fixture, no wet cabinet, no wall moisture, no exterior pooling. The visible unit meter also showed no movement during a 20-minute no-use check.

Management replied 2025-02-18: the billed meter number matches the unit, and management's records show no building-side leak or estimated read for the statement period. Management will only request a utility reread if given meter photos taken before and after an 8-hour no-use interval. Any flush, dishwasher run, washing-machine run, or fridge water dispensing during that window invalidates the interval.

2025-02-19 update: Sam and I completed the required 8-hour no-use interval (9:00am–5:00pm), handling Kibo's bowl/bathroom needs beforehand and avoiding all faucets, toilets, dishwasher, washing machine, and fridge dispenser during the window. Before/after meter photos both read 003912.4 — no movement. Uploaded photos and test log through Cherrywood's resident portal; utility reread is now pending.

2025-02-22 update: Cherrywood reviewed the portal submission, accepted the 8-hour no-use interval as valid, and opened utility reread ticket CW-2025-218. January usage remains under review; no adjustment made yet. Management estimates a response in ten business days and will not close the case until the utility returns meter history and reread result. The 3,360-gallon Dec→Jan increase remains disputed pending that response.

2025-03-09 update: February billed at 3,180 gallons over 28 days (~113.6 gal/day), close to December's ~100.6 gal/day and roughly half January's ~209.7 gal/day rate — so usage returned to normal the month after the spike, meaning January now reads as an isolated event rather than an ongoing household leak. Utility reread under ticket CW-2025-218 came back: no continuous-flow pattern found, and the current meter was confirmed accurate — but the utility could not retrospectively validate the specific January reading itself. So the reread clears the meter/plumbing of an ongoing fault without confirming or refuting that the January number was correct. User and Sam have asked Cherrywood management to adjust the disputed 6,480-gallon January charge; management's decision on the adjustment is pending.

2025-03-24 update: Cherrywood responded with a partial-credit calculation rather than a full adjustment. It treats the 3,360-gallon Dec→Jan increase as disputed, splits it down the middle, and credits only half (1,680 gallons) at a combined water-and-sewer rate of $0.0125/gallon — a $21.00 credit. Management's only stated basis for the 50/50 split is uncertainty about the source of the January usage; it offers no evidence assigning the other half to the household. User and Sam have not accepted the offer and continue to dispute the remaining $21.00, while keeping the no-late-action hold in place.

**Why:** Since the in-unit meter didn't move during the 8-hour no-use test, the current meter checks out as accurate, and usage normalized the very next month, the weight of evidence points to January being a one-off anomaly (misread, transient event, or billing error) rather than a real or ongoing leak — but because the utility can't retroactively validate that specific January reading, there's no hard proof either way. Cherrywood's 50/50 split credit isn't grounded in evidence either — it's an unexplained compromise, not a finding that half the usage was the household's.

2025-03-27 update: Cherrywood applied the $21.00 credit for 1,680 gallons but declined the remaining $21.00, again citing uncertainty about January's source without adding meter or household-use evidence. The remaining $21.00 is now coded as disputed, will not accrue late fees, and will stay out of collection while a regional manager reviews the final request by 2025-04-04.

2025-04-04 final update: The regional manager reviewed the Dec/Jan/Feb comparison, the unchanged 8-hour no-use test, and the utility reread, and found no evidence assigning January's isolated 3,360-gallon increase to the household. The remaining $21.00 was credited at the same $0.0125/gallon rate, bringing the total credit to $42.00 — the full disputed amount. No late fee or collections balance exists, and management left no unresolved household-leak claim on file. Case closed.

**How to apply:** Dispute fully resolved — full $42.00 credited, no admission or finding of a household leak either way. No further action needed. Related: [[project_cherrywood_lease_renewal_decision]], [[project_cherrywood_bike_tag_resolution]].

"Current active Customer Success adoption or renewal work is a valid suppression. Stale, unresolved, or conflicting required state creates a field-specific hold until a fresh source check and system reevaluation; Operations does not manually release it. External-system authority means readiness to perform the connector's required owner-level permission or network-allowlist action, not permission for automated contact."

On 2025-05-16, Customer Success reported that the one-page operator glossary's individual definitions were clear but suppression and hold still looked operationally similar without worked examples. Updated the glossary with two de-identified, side-by-side examples:

1. Suppression: an account passing all evaluation preconditions but with active CS adoption/renewal work open — suppressed as a valid final resting state until CS closes that work, not an error or defect.
2. Hold: the real 2025-05-15 case from [[project_cs_auto_nudge_scheduled_decision_duplicate_records_may2025]] — a stale required governed field (no CS work involved) produces a visible, field-specific hold until a fresh source check succeeds, which triggers automatic system reevaluation.

Both entries state explicitly that neither outcome is manually released — suppression clears only when CS closes its own work, and holds clear only via the automated fresh-source-check-and-reevaluation cycle, never by operator override.

The glossary update also reinforced, per [[project_cs_tooltip_authority_outreach_conflation_apr2025]], that external-system authority describes connector readiness — whether an owner can complete the required owner-level permission or network-allowlist action — and is not permission for automated outreach; this distinction was called out again here because authority state can surface near hold/suppression language and risks the same conflation.

**Why:** Same fault line as [[project_cs_auto_nudge_ines_messaging_state_draft_may2025]] — suppression (CS-caused, valid business state) and hold (source-staleness-caused, fail-closed) keep getting conflated by people operating the CS auto-nudge system, even after individually-correct glossary definitions. Pairing definitions with contrasting, de-identified examples and naming that neither is manually released addresses why operators kept treating them as interchangeable or overridable.

**How to apply:** When explaining suppression vs. hold to CS or other operators, always pair the definitions with contrasting worked examples rather than definitions alone, and state plainly that neither is manually released. Reinforce: CS activity never triggers a hold, stale data never triggers suppression, and external-authority/connector-readiness never implies automated-outreach consent — see [[project_cs_tooltip_authority_outreach_conflation_apr2025]] for the standing rule on that last point.

metadata:

---

Customer.io product notice (received 2024-12-06): effective Jan 15, 2025, Liquid's `default` filter will treat whitespace-only strings as empty (currently treated as present, so the fallback never fires). Ines flagged several routine templates use `default` for optional company names and could be affected.

Owner split (per [[project-helio-start-owner-lanes-mar2024]] pattern — Ines=lifecycle copy/risk controls, Daniela=eng/release control):
- Ines: copy review, sampling live data for whitespace-only occurrences, pre/post-cutover preflight comparisons on affected templates.
- Shared/first step: full inventory of templates using `default` on any optional field (not just company name) — needed before scoping further work.
- Daniela: any actual template logic fix (e.g., `strip` before `default`) or source-level data cleanup, plus release timing for those fixes ahead of the Jan 15 cutover.

**Why:** External platform behavior change with a hard cutover date and a real (if narrow) customer-facing rendering risk — worth tracking so the Jan 15 deadline and the inventory/fix split don't get lost.
**How to apply:** Before Jan 15, 2025, confirm template inventory is complete and that any templates needing behavior preservation (not just copy tweaks) have a Daniela-owned fix scheduled. Treat plain copy adjustments as Ines's routine lane, no escalation needed.

**Jan 14, 2025 final preview matrix (Ines), day ahead of cutover:**
- Renewal reminder: null → "your workspace"; whitespace-only → "your workspace"; populated → company name.
- Integration summary: same pattern as renewal reminder.
- Monthly workspace digest: already applies a trim/strip before `default`, so whitespace-only collapses to empty pre-cutover and already renders "your workspace" — this template's behavior isn't changing on Jan 15, unlike the other two, which pick up the new whitespace-only fallback for the first time on cutover.
All three templates confirmed producing the intended fallback ahead of the Jan 15 cutover; no Daniela logic fix needed for these three (they end up correct either via the native filter change itself or the pre-existing trim).

**Boundary rule (recorded on test plan, 1-14-25):** if an unexpected rendering result turns up post-cutover, hold only the affected template and route the fix to Daniela — do not pause unrelated lifecycle sends.

**Jan 15, 2025 cutover-day finding (Ines, first production preview):** a nonbreaking space (not caught by the 1-14 test matrix, which only covered null and ordinary whitespace) survives Liquid's `default` filter as non-empty and renders "Hi ," instead of falling back to "your workspace team" — found via an imported company-name value. Applying the boundary rule above: only the renewal reminder is held pending a Daniela fix; integration summary, monthly workspace digest, and unrelated lifecycle sends render correctly and remain active.
**Why:** The 1-14 preview matrix tested null/whitespace but missed the nonbreaking-space edge case, so "no Daniela fix needed" from that matrix is now superseded for the renewal reminder specifically.
**How to apply:** Treat renewal reminder as open/blocked (needs a Daniela fix, likely a stricter strip/normalize before `default`) until confirmed patched; don't extend the hold to the other two templates.

**Diagnostic next step (2025-01-15):** Since integration summary shares "the same pattern as renewal reminder" per the 1-14 matrix, it may carry the same latent nonbreaking-space exposure. Recommended: Ines spot-checks integration summary sends for the same case in parallel — a look, not a hold — since it hasn't produced its own confirmed rendering failure. Don't preemptively hold it on the strength of the shared pattern alone.

**Resolution (2025-01-16, Daniela/Ines): CLOSED.** Daniela traced the root cause to an imported nonbreaking-space value that bypassed the template's ordinary trim step; her team normalized that value before the Liquid `default` filter evaluates it. Ines re-ran fresh previews (null, ordinary whitespace, nonbreaking space, populated) — all empty variants now render "your workspace," populated stays unchanged. Ines released the held renewal reminder under her standing routine authority (per [[project-helio-start-owner-lanes-mar2024]] lane split). No unrelated template was paused or changed.
**Why:** Closes the boundary-rule hold opened on cutover day; confirms the fix addresses the actual root cause (upstream data, not just filter behavior) rather than papering over the symptom.
**How to apply:** Treat renewal reminder as fixed and active, not open/blocked. The integration-summary spot-check recommendation above is superseded/moot unless a separate nonbreaking-space failure surfaces there independently — the underlying data-import cause is now normalized upstream of all templates.

On 2024-06-13, Priya asked the user to turn their H2 ownership commitment into a repeatable kickoff check to run before any query or dashboard is built for evidence work, rather than leaving it as a general intention. The checklist drafted:

1. Assign the metric-definition owner (distinct from whoever writes the query).
2. Settle timestamp semantics up front (e.g., settlement vs. authorization) and confirm in writing.
3. Identify Finance dependencies early, including expected turnaround, whenever money/refunds/settlement windows are involved.
4. Name implementation and validation owners separately — never the same person as sole validator.
5. Record unresolved assumptions (denominator scope, cohort window, edge cases) as a visible list, revisited at the readout.
6. Every continuous-control source and owner certification must state an exact through-date — no open-ended or implied coverage windows.
7. Normalize UTC timestamps to the named business time zone before comparing dates across sources.
8. The review must remain incomplete whenever source coverage and owner certification do not match exactly — a normalized, exact match is required to close, not an approximate or "close enough" one.

**Why:** Items 1–5 are directly motivated by the [[project_helio_start_first_paid_measurement_audit]] gap (settlement vs. authorization timestamp ambiguity, Finance dependency surfacing late) and echo Owen's own internalized "opening block" habit from [[project_owen_performance_review_jan2024]] — this generalizes that individual discipline into a team-level kickoff step under [[project_priya_remit_expansion_mar2024]]. Items 6–8 were added on 2026-10-13, when the user and Owen used the unresolved [[project_owen_october_source_completeness_review_oct2026]] discrepancy (a same-instant timezone-formatting artifact that looked like a real gap, plus CS certification genuinely lagging at Sept 29 vs. the Sept 30 through-date the other sources reconciled to) to generalize the lesson into the standing checklist, without changing anyone's authority.

**How to apply:** Use this checklist at the start of any new evidence/measurement work (query or dashboard build) going forward. Treat it as the user's own standing practice, not a mandatory companywide template — same spirit as [[project_investigation_framework_standing_practice]] (lightweight, not a centralized approval gate). This checklist update does not itself close the October CS auto-nudge packet or change claim, board-readiness, or source-closure authority — Owen keeps that packet marked incomplete until Customer Success recertifies an exact September 30, 2026 through-date.

name: project_expansion_assist_concurrent_adoption_case_attribution
description: "2024-09-16: in-window help request + in-window expansion that occur during a post-exposure CS adoption case — logged normally in the primary window, but expansion is annotated as non-attributable to the prompt"
metadata:

On 2024-09-16, Owen found another Expansion Assist boundary case: at exposure-time eligibility check there was no active CS adoption/renewal case, so the exposure was valid. CS opened an adoption case 8 days post-exposure. The account then requested help on day 10 (in-window) and an expansion became effective on day 31 (also in-window, since 31 < 45).

Rule: because both the help request and the expansion fall inside the 45-day window (unlike [[project_expansion_assist_delayed_outcome_split_window_treatment]], where the outcome landed outside it), both are logged normally in the primary maturation outcome table for this account — they are not stripped out or moved to a secondary/descriptive log. The post-exposure adoption case is logged separately per [[project_expansion_assist_post_exposure_adoption_suppression]] (forward suppression only, no retroactive invalidation of the exposure). The expansion record is annotated to make the concurrent adoption case visible, and explicitly is not characterized as resulting from the Expansion Assist prompt — CS-driven adoption work was independently underway before the expansion matured.

**Why:** Preserves exposure-time eligibility semantics (fail-closed, no retroactive suppression) while avoiding a false causal read: an in-window expansion that happens during active, independently-initiated CS work shouldn't be presented as prompt-driven just because it falls inside the maturation window. Matches the standing no-causal/no-pipeline-credit discipline in [[project_expansion_assist_pilot_approval_jul8_2024]].

**How to apply:** When an in-window request and/or in-window expansion co-occur with a post-exposure CS adoption/renewal case: (1) keep the exposure and eligibility determination unchanged; (2) log the CS case as its own post-exposure event triggering forward suppression only; (3) include the in-window request and in-window expansion in the primary outcome table (do not exclude just because CS activity overlaps); (4) annotate the expansion record noting the concurrent CS case and explicitly disclaiming attribution to the prompt; (5) treat as a single observational case — no change to the aggregate pilot read, which remains incomplete pending full cohort maturation.

name: project_expansion_assist_delayed_outcome_split_window_treatment
description: "2024-09-11: help request inside the 45-day window can have its resulting expansion mature outside it — request and outcome are classified separately, not as one unit"
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: project
  originSessionId: 03d0d2fe-367b-4f07-bb8e-717a159698cb
  modified: 2026-09-17T17:43:33.530Z
---

On 2024-09-11, Owen found a boundary case while validating already-completed Expansion Assist exposures: an account's options-review help request landed 12 hours post-exposure (inside the 45-day window), but the resulting expansion became effective 46 days 19 hours post-exposure (outside the window, by elapsed instant per [[project_expansion_assist_timezone_window_classification_rule]]). Not a duplicate request, not a new exposure.

Rule: the help request and its eventual commercial outcome are classified independently against the 45-day window, not bundled as one event. The request (in-window) is logged as a valid post-exposure handoff per [[project_expansion_assist_post_exposure_help_reply_handoff]]. The expansion (out-of-window) is excluded from the primary 45-day maturation numerator/denominator, but its raw timestamps and CS record are preserved in the descriptive/secondary outcome log, annotated as a later-maturing outcome originating from an in-window request — not deleted, not merged into the primary read.

**Why:** A request can be a legitimate in-window response to exposure while the deal it triggers still takes longer than 45 days to close. Counting the outcome in the primary window would overstate what the 45-day read is designed to measure; discarding it entirely would lose a real, later commercial outcome tied to the pilot. Splitting the two preserves both the window's integrity and the full record.

**How to apply:** For any case where a post-exposure request falls inside 45 days but its resulting outcome (expansion, cancellation, etc.) matures after: (1) classify the request against the window on its own elapsed-instant timestamp; (2) classify the outcome against the window on its own elapsed-instant timestamp, independently; (3) if the outcome falls outside, keep it out of the primary window's count but log it in the descriptive/secondary table with a note connecting it back to the in-window request; (4) no causal or pipeline claim from a single case — this stays observational, consistent with [[project_expansion_assist_pilot_approval_jul8_2024]] and [[project_helio_start_paid_acquisition_evidence_bar_aug2024]].

6-24-24: Owen's fixture-only dry run of the approved Expansion Assist eligibility query (see [[project_expansion_assist_pilot_approval_jul8_2024]]) found the "recent active admin" readiness signal was overstated three ways:
1. Service-token/API activity was counting as human-admin activity (masking a stale real admin).
2. No staleness cutoff was enforced — any human-admin timestamp, however old, passed.
3. Suppression check relied only on the nightly snapshot, missing same-day CS actions not yet reflected in the table.

Corrected logic:
- Recent-active-admin signal requires a human admin session (exclude service tokens) within a freshness window — recommended 30 days, pending metric-owner confirmation.

- Suppression check must fail-closed per [[project_expansion_assist_freshness_failclosed_rule]]: known in-flight CS work not yet reflected in the nightly table routes to hold queue, never defaults to eligible.

**Why:** This was a fixture-only dry run, not a live-account check — no exposure or scheduling change before the 7-8-24 launch. The fix closes gaps that would have silently over-admitted accounts into the pilot's 30-acct behavior-readiness cap.

**How to apply:** When Expansion Assist eligibility/QA work comes up again, treat human-vs-service-token distinction, the staleness cutoff, and same-day suppression lag as permanent regression fixtures, not one-off dry-run cases.

**How to apply:** Report these numbers as final descriptive results only, always specifying which denominator (locked-primary ITT vs actual-exposure) a given expansion count refers to, and never collapsing the 12-account subgroup result into a conversion-rate percentage. Priya selected a randomized stagger design for the proposed 30-account Expansion Assist pilot: 5 eligible accounts begin each week for 6 weeks, with start order randomized before launch. Accounts not yet started in a given week serve as temporary comparisons until their assigned start week.

Owen must model calendar week and exposure time explicitly in the measurement design. Customer Success remains limited to 5 newly exposed accounts per week (matches the stagger, not a separate constraint).

**Why:** Keeps the pilot analyzable (randomized order + explicit time/exposure modeling) while bounding CS load and avoiding early causal claims from a small, staggered rollout.

**How to apply:** No live prompt may be sent before 2024-07-08. Exposed-account outcomes alone do not authorize a causal claim — any read of pilot results should stay descriptive until the full design (all 6 cohorts, comparison structure) is complete. Keep in line with [[feedback_riley_mrr_snapshot_framing]] and [[feedback_planning_revenue_framing]]: Expansion Assist stays out of revenue/launch language regardless of pilot progress.

**2024-05-10 attrition/replacement design (Owen's question):** Eligibility locks at randomization — all 30 accounts stay in the primary intent-to-treat analysis by original assigned start week regardless of pre-exposure churn, downgrade out of retained-mid, or competing sales-led expansion contact. Those events are labeled/flagged in Owen's model (separate categories, descriptive only), never used to drop or swap accounts out of the primary 30. Any replacement need is served by a separately randomized reserve pool, set up in advance and analyzed on its own — never merged into the primary comparison.

**2024-05-14 Priya-accepted implementation rules (finalizes the above):** The primary 30-account cohort is locked and randomized together before launch and stays in the primary intent-to-treat analysis regardless of what happens pre-exposure. Specific event labels: churn or loss of retained-mid eligibility before exposure → "eligibility loss without exposure"; entry into a sales-led expansion conversation before exposure → "competing event" (never silently removed). A separately randomized reserve list may replace an account operationally, filled in original reserve order, but reserve accounts must always be reported separately from the primary 30, never merged in. CS exposure cap confirmed at 5 new accounts/week. Earliest live date stays 2024-07-08; this remains design work only, not authorization to send prompts.

**2024-05-28 assignment-visibility protocol (implementation update only):** Tiered access to the randomized assignment file — Owen retains full visibility into the complete file; a designated CS operations lead sees only a rolling 7-day-ahead window of upcoming assignments; an assigned frontline rep sees a given account no earlier than 24 hours before its scheduled exposure. Pre-exposure records shown to any of these narrower views use neutral labels (no treatment/control language), while ordinary support information for those accounts remains fully available regardless of visibility tier. Owen reviews the access log weekly. Does not change the primary intent-to-treat cohort, the separately randomized reserve list, the 5-account/week CS exposure cap, or the 2024-07-08 earliest-live boundary — this is an access-control implementation detail only and still does not authorize sending a live prompt.

**2024-05-30 permission test passed (issue resolved):** Owen and the designated CS operations lead ran the restricted staging-sheet permission test — confirmed Owen sees the full assignment file, the ops lead sees only the next 7 days, and a frontline test user sees no future assignments and only the account scheduled within 24 hours. Neutral pre-exposure labels and the weekly access log also verified working as specified. Assignment-visibility implementation issue is now closed. No prompt sent, no account exposed; 2024-07-08 earliest-live boundary and 5-account/week cap remain unchanged.

**2024-06-12 shadow-review evidence and eligibility/copy design rules (see [[project_expansion_assist_shadow_review_jun2024]] and [[project_expansion_assist_candidate_suppression_and_copy_rule]]):** Owen's closed six-month shadow-review export covered a 240-account population. Within that population, 46 accounts showed all three behavior signals (deeper integration use, recent active-admin behavior, and a product-visible usage ceiling); 17 of those 46 expanded within 45 days, versus 11 of the other 194. Of the 46 flagged accounts, CS's individual review found 9 with active adoption or renewal work underway and suppressed them from any candidate list — a commercial prompt would be inappropriate while that work is in progress. Eligible-candidate definition for the pilot is therefore: all three behavior signals present, AND no active CS adoption/renewal work (else suppressed). Ines separately confirmed that any lifecycle/in-product copy must describe the account's current state (e.g. observed usage/adoption signals), never fixed signup age, as the reason to act.

**Why:** This shadow-review is descriptive/observational only — accounts were not randomized or prompted, so the 37.0% vs 5.7% association is background signal, not causal evidence of lift and not forecast credit. It informs which accounts qualify as candidates and how copy should be framed, but changes nothing about the pilot's causal design.

**How to apply:** Keep the shadow-review numbers and the eligibility/suppression/copy rules fully separate from causal claims. The locked 30-account primary intent-to-treat cohort, the separately randomized reserve pool, the 5-account/week CS exposure cap, the tiered assignment-visibility controls, and the 2024-07-08 earliest-live boundary are all unchanged by this update — this is candidate-definition and copy-design input, not authorization to launch or a basis for rollout/access-widening language (consistent with [[feedback_beta_chart_framing]]).

**2024-06-14 Owen's question, resolved for the 2024-06-18 review:** Owen asked whether the 37 accounts left after removing the 9 CS-suppressed accounts from the 46 flagged accounts should replace the already-randomized 30-account primary cohort. Answer: no. The 37 is a snapshot from the closed 2024-06-12 historical shadow-review population — a fixed, past-dated retrospective count, not a live, currently-eligible candidate list. CS adoption/renewal status and behavior signals can change between now and any actual exposure date, so candidate status must be reevaluated near exposure, not taken as fixed from 6/12. The primary 30 was locked and randomized before this shadow-review candidate work existed; splicing in a differently-derived list would break the randomization the ITT analysis depends on. The two pre-exposure eligibility losses already in the locked 30 keep their "eligibility loss without exposure" label and stay in the primary ITT analysis — they are not backfilled from the 37 or from anywhere else. Any replacement need is still served only by the separately randomized reserve list in its original reserve order, reported separately from the primary 30 — never by pulling from the shadow-review population.

**Why:** Protects the causal integrity of the locked randomization and keeps historical/observational shadow-review output from silently becoming a live operational list.

**How to apply:** If this question resurfaces (e.g. a fresher shadow-review cut, or pressure to "top up" the 30 with well-performing historical accounts), reapply this same reasoning: recompute eligibility near exposure, never touch the locked 30 or reserve order, keep labels as-is.

**2024-06-20 first reserve fill (Owen's cohort update):** Owen applied the approved rules to the locked primary cohort: the two pre-exposure eligibility losses remain labeled as such, leaving 28 currently-eligible primary accounts and 2 open operational slots. In the reserve list, reserve 1 currently has active renewal work underway and is suppressed under the same active-adoption/renewal rule as [[project_expansion_assist_candidate_suppression_and_copy_rule]] — held in its reserve position, not deleted or skipped permanently. Reserve 2 and reserve 3 currently pass all three behavior signals with no active suppression, so they fill the two open slots next in original reserve order. Operational/exposed cohort size stays at 30 (28 primary + 2 reserve), and reserve-filled accounts are reported as their own line, never merged into the primary 30's numbers.

**Why:** Applies the 2024-05-14 reserve-order rule and the CS suppression rule together without rewriting the locked primary ITT or exceeding the 30-account operational cap; keeps reserve 1 available rather than silently dropping it if its renewal work clears before exposure.

**How to apply:** Treat reserve status as re-checked at each fill point, not fixed — reserve 1 stays first in line for any future opening and should be reevaluated for suppression status again close to the 2024-07-08 exposure date, same as any other candidate.

**2024-07-01 final live rerun with validated current-user-status join (see [[project_expansion_assist_eligibility_recency_bugfix]]):** Owen's final live rerun, now using the corrected current-user-status join (human-vs-token distinction, staleness cutoff, current suppression table), confirms 28 eligible locked-primary accounts — unchanged from the 2024-06-20 count. Reserve 1 remains suppressed for active renewal work; reserves 2 and 3 remain available and fill the two open operational slots, also unchanged. Daniela independently validated the join against a labeled fixture suite: A and F pass eligibility. B fails — activity is service-token-only, not human-admin. C fails — human-admin activity is stale (past the recency cutoff). D fails — current renewal work is active (CS suppression rule). E fails — the usage-ceiling behavior signal is missing. G fails — the human admin who generated the recent activity is now deactivated. Stale or conflicting adoption/renewal records fail closed (never default into the eligible/candidate set), consistent with [[project_expansion_assist_freshness_failclosed_rule]].

**Why:** Confirms the bugfixed join reproduces the same operational cohort (28 primary + reserves 2/3) as before the fix, while the fixture suite demonstrates the corrected logic now correctly excludes token-only activity, stale admin activity, active renewal work, missing ceiling signal, and deactivated admins — closing the three overstatement paths Owen's dry run found on 2024-06-24.

**How to apply:** This is still designed status, not launch — no exposure has occurred and the 2024-07-08 earliest-live boundary is unchanged. Do not claim any account has been exposed or that the pilot has started. Cite the A–G fixture results as validation evidence for the join logic, not as new eligibility findings (the 28/reserve counts were already established 2024-06-20). Keep fail-closed behavior (B, C, D, E, G) as the standing pattern for any future join changes.

name: project_expansion_assist_timezone_window_classification_rule
description: "2024-09-04: 45-day maturation window classified by actual elapsed time from exposure instant, not by calendar date shown on any dashboard/timezone"
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: project
  originSessionId: 30314bf5-9507-4996-968b-bc4c2f87268f
  modified: 2026-09-17T17:28:01.986Z
---

On 2024-09-04, during Expansion Assist maturation QA, Owen found a help request whose source event fired at 11:58pm Pacific but lands on the following calendar date in the warehouse's UTC-based dashboard. The exposure timestamp and raw channel event are both intact; this is not a new exposure and not a duplicate request (see [[project_expansion_assist_exposure_counting_rule]] for the account-level dedup rule this doesn't touch).

Rule: whether a request/outcome falls inside the approved 45-day window is determined by actual elapsed wall-clock time between the exposure instant and the event instant (both as absolute timestamps, e.g. UTC epoch/instant comparison) — never by comparing calendar-date labels as rendered by a particular dashboard or timezone setting. A dashboard showing the event on "day 46" purely because its display timezone rolled the date forward does not move the event outside the window if the true elapsed time is within 45 days.

**Why:** Calendar-date display is timezone-dependent and can shift an event's apparent date without changing how much time actually elapsed since exposure — using displayed date instead of elapsed instant risk misclassifying borderline requests right at the window edge, which would corrupt the 45-day maturation read this cohort depends on.

**How to apply:** For any Expansion Assist window/maturation classification, compute elapsed time from the stored exposure timestamp to the stored event timestamp as absolute instants, not from whatever calendar date a UTC- or Pacific-rendered dashboard shows. Retain both the raw local-timezone event record and its UTC equivalent as evidence (neither is discarded or normalized away). This is a classification-rule fix only — no new exposure, no duplicate count, and no complete outcome table is being reported here (contrast with the finished day-90 table in [[project_helio_start_first_paid_measurement_audit]]).

On 2024-05-14, the abandoned-intake reminder audience query was corrected: eligibility requires BOTH (1) intake start is older than 24 hours AND (2) the submission has no final route (final route is null). Workspace ID alone is not a valid eligibility test.

QA matrix (all states must pass before going live):
- Admitted → excluded (final admitted route exists)
- Assisted → excluded (final assisted route exists)
- Ineligible → excluded (final ineligible route exists)
- Abandoned before a final route, >24h old → included (genuinely unfinished intake)
- Pending connector access → excluded/kept in assisted sequence, not treated as abandoned

The query must evaluate the *final* route after provisional events resolve — a submission that looks unfinished early but later finalizes as admitted/assisted/ineligible must still be excluded.

**Why:** Prevents false-positive abandoned-intake reminders being sent to workspaces that are actually mid-assist (e.g. pending connector credentials, see [[project_helio_start_connector_credential_two_week_read]]) or already finalized through a different route.

**How to apply:** No live reminder should ship until Ines implements this exact logic and reruns the fixtures above with all five states passing. Treat this as a hard gate — don't advise sending reminders based on workspace ID or intake age alone.

**Update (2024-05-16):** Gate cleared. All 42 routing fixtures covering the five states passed, including transitions that finalize after an earlier provisional event. No live reminder was sent under the faulty query prior to this fix. Ines is clear to ship the corrected live reminder.

**Update (2024-06-04):** New blocking bug found in a separate pre-send QA pass — the bounded through-Q3 footer is nested inside an admission-state conditional, so it renders correctly for admitted/assisted/ineligible fixtures but is hidden for the pending-connector fixture (HTML and plain text). No affected message has sent. Release is blocked again until Ines moves the footer outside the conditional and reruns admitted/assisted/ineligible/pending-connector fixtures in both HTML and plain text.

**Update (2024-06-05):** Fixed. Ines moved the footer outside the admission-state conditional and reran all four fixtures (admitted, assisted, ineligible, pending-connector) in both HTML and plain text — all eight renderings show consistent through-Q3 wording with no admission or same-day workspace-creation promises. Release unblocked; cleared to ship.

**Update (2024-06-10):** Third bug found and fixed — the audience preview was built from a stale snapshot, so 14 applicants who had since finalized to assisted or ineligible were still being included. Ines implemented send-time final-state suppression (re-evaluates final route at send time, not from the earlier snapshot) and reran the audience preview: all 14 stale-state applicants removed; pending-connector cases, admitted workspaces, and all other completed final routes confirmed excluded; genuinely incomplete applications remain included. No reminder sent from the faulty snapshot. Corrected audience is ready for the scheduled release.

As of 2023-09-08, the Helio Start intake flow moved the admin-ownership proof step to *before* workspace setup, replacing reliance on after-the-fact lifecycle copy. Ines drafted three candidate intake lines; user rejected options that either (a) let unclear-admin accounts continue into the beta path, or (b) read like legal attestation language.

Agreed copy principle: the intake line must be a real gate (stops flow on "no"), stay conversational/friendly (no "certify"/"attest" language), and be honest that ownership can't be reassigned once the workspace exists — no promise that later messaging can fix it.

**Why:** ties directly to [[project_admin_role_permission_confusion]] (2023-08-25 beta viewers blocked on API-key gen) — the fix path shifted from downstream lifecycle messaging to upstream intake filtering.

**How to apply:** when reviewing future Helio Start onboarding/intake copy, check it against this three-part test (hard gate / friendly tone / no false promise of later fixability) before treating it as done.

2023-09-12: Daniela proposed how to verify the admin-ownership claim behind the intake gate, not just the copy. Three options: (1) self-reported form attestation at invite acceptance — fastest, ships this sprint, but unverified; (2) OAuth scope check after first connection attempt — more reliable where integrations expose scope, but happens after setup has started and is integration-dependent; (3) CS confirms admin owner pre-invite — cleanest but CS can't staff a manual pre-clear queue. Daniela's recommendation, adopted: ship (1) this sprint instrumented as `admin_proof_attested`, layer in (2) later as a validation signal where available, and hold (3) in reserve only if the beta cap tightens further.

2023-09-12 (admin-proof huddle, refines above): confirmed the chosen path is *not* a CS pre-clear queue for every invite. Working path: attestation at invite acceptance for all candidates, with CS routing added only as a branch for candidates who self-report being unsure who owns admin access (a lighter-weight version of option 3, folded into option 1 rather than replacing it). Owen wants the `admin_proof_attested` field surfaced in his beta readouts. Ines is holding the intake copy (see three-part test above) until the event name is finalized. Daniela owes a confirmation by 2023-09-13 on whether `admin_proof_attested` can be logged at invite acceptance and wired into the beta dashboard without touching billing-state work — this is the pending blocker on both Owen's readout and Ines's copy sign-off.

2023-09-13: Daniela confirmed the implementation path — blocker cleared. `admin_proof_attested` will be emitted at invite acceptance and exposed to Owen's beta dashboard without touching billing-state work. Field is `true` when the invitee confirms admin access, `unsure` when they don't; `unsure` routes to CS before setup rather than letting the workspace get created first. Caveat: invitations sent before the patch may show `null` until the invitee reopens the acceptance step. Ines can now finalize intake copy against this event name; Owen can add the field to Monday's (2023-09-18) readout.

2023-09-13, three candidate lines reviewed: (A) "I confirm I can manage admin settings for this workspace and can connect the first integration without another team's approval" — accepted for the `true` branch, plain and non-legalese. (B) "I attest that I am the authorized administrator..." — rejected, repeats the "attest"/legalese language already ruled out. (C) "Not sure who owns admin settings? You can still continue, and our team may follow up if setup needs extra help." — flagged as broken: it tells the user they can "still continue" when `unsure` is actually supposed to route to CS before setup starts, so the copy overpromises relative to actual behavior. Needs a rewrite before sign-off (something like "we'll confirm access with you before setup continues," not "still continue").

2023-09-14: Daniela pushed the invite-acceptance patch live for new Helio Start beta invites. Owen can now see the `admin_proof_attested` field in his beta dashboard (will be sparse until new invitations are accepted). Ines swapped in the final corrected intake line for the `unsure` branch, routing to the assisted/CS path before setup rather than the rejected "still continue" framing. Implementation question is no longer blocked — event name, intake copy, and dashboard field are all aligned.

2023-09-22 (Friday beta read, Owen's numbers): since the patch went live, 15 invitees have accepted — 10 selected `admin_proof_attested=true`, 5 selected `unsure` and were routed to CS before setup, confirming the gate branches as designed. Live beta is 18 active accounts with 15 de-duped first-integration attempts. Support log totals 30 questions (12 permissions/admin-ownership, 6 billing-expectation, 4 import/migration, 8 ordinary setup); only 3 new since Wednesday (1 permissions question from a shared-admin alias, 2 ordinary setup, both docs-first). User drafted Priya's exec-note bullets from this data, deliberately holding the line against any implication of pricing-page readiness, wider invitation volume, or revenue motion — consistent with [[feedback_tomas_beta_read_framing]] and [[feedback_beta_chart_framing]].

2026-09-26: leadership planning session ended with neither Tomás nor Priya asking to widen Helio Start, put it on the pricing page, or count the admin-proof step as an activation win — the held line above worked. User's internal note this week frames admin proof as a quality gate routing unclear ownership before setup (not an eligibility failure, per [[feedback_tomas_beta_read_framing]]), while explicitly flagging the evidence as still early and the beta as still capped.

2023-10-03: Ines applied the safer lifecycle wording to the final Customer.io preview for the next controlled-beta invitation batch, closing the outstanding copy concern. Final lines: "Before you set up your workspace, confirm the person accepting this invite controls admin access for the tools you plan to connect." and "If you need CSV import, migration help, or manual billing, reply here and we'll route you to the assisted path before setup." User reviewed and approved; told Ines to queue it for the next batch.

2023-10-11 (Wednesday 72-hour read, 34-recipient batch from [[project_customerio_suppression_mismatch]]): Owen's numbers — 24 acceptances (17 `admin_proof_attested=true`, 7 `unsure` routed to CS before setup), 14 workspaces created, 10 de-duped first-integration attempts. Support log: 10 questions — only 2 permissions/admin-ownership (a shared-admin-alias case plus a new edge-case type, agency-admin-after-attestation, where the attester wasn't the actual account owner), 8 ordinary API-key/setup handled docs-first. Two hard bounces still excluded from the acceptance denominator; no manual billing/import rows. Priya asked if admin proof can be called "working" in Friday's exec note; user's answer: yes as a quality gate (correctly routing unclear ownership pre-setup, keeping permissions load thin), explicitly not as evidence the admin path is clean or ready to widen — the two edge cases show it still needs manual judgment on ambiguous ownership.

**Why:** Same no-widening-signal boundary as [[feedback_beta_chart_framing]] and the Sept 28/Sept 26 reads in [[project_helio_start_beta_read_data_sept28]] — "working" describes the gate's function, not the state of the admin path overall.

**How to apply:** When Priya, Tomás, or others ask to characterize admin-proof results going forward, keep the same split: gate mechanics can be called working/functioning; overall admin-path readiness or invite-pool widening cannot be inferred from batch-level support-question counts. Watch the agency-admin-after-attestation pattern for recurrence — it's a new edge-case shape distinct from the shared-admin-alias and inherited-integration cases already tracked.

2023-11-13: Second occurrence of the agency-admin-after-attestation edge case (first seen 2023-10-11) — a Nov batch account attested `true`, but CS got a reply revealing the customer's outside agency actually controls admin access. Handled by pulling the account off self-serve, routing to the assisted-setup path (same as an `unsure` branch), and explicitly declining to invent an exception letting the agency complete the step directly — that would recreate the pre-setup ownership-verification gap the intake gate exists to close. Told Owen not to count it as a clean admin-confirmed activation in the dashboard. With two instances now, this may warrant its own tracked subtype rather than being folded into "edge cases" generally — worth revisiting if a third occurs.

2023-11-27: CS categorized the six November invitees routed to CS before setup (the `unsure`/ambiguous branch): 3 said they were not the workspace owner, 1 was the shared-agency OAuth-domain case (recurring type, see 2023-10-11/11-13 above), 1 was unsure because SSO ownership sat with IT, 1 had delegated setup to a contractor. None were manual-billing or import requests. For the January readiness conversation ([[project_admin_confirmation_event_stability]]): this confirms the gate is doing its intended job of catching non-owner acceptances and keeping billing/import out of the CS-routed pool, but admin proof itself — reliably identifying the true owner up front — is still the open problem, not a solved one.

2023-12-15: Owen's combined Oct+Nov controlled-batch rollup — 50 accepted invitees, 34 confirmed admin ownership, 16 routed to CS pre-setup, 22 new workspaces, 19 reaching first integration. Daniela confirmed entitlement/support-state tagging ([[project_entitlement_support_state_enum]]) stays clean for new rows; Ines confirmed the conservative lifecycle fork keeps holding, conditioned on the unsupported-list staying explicit; CS confirmed no admitted manual-billing/import tickets in the Q4 batches. Marcus Vail asked whether this closeout could be phrased as setup for a Q1 launch. Riley's decision: this is a January readiness gate, not a December launch claim — support-load, admin-proof, entitlement-instrumentation, and unsupported-list all remain open conditions, none resolved by this rollup.

**Why:** Marcus's launch-framing ask is the same recurring pattern tracked in [[project_q4_forecast_helio_narrative]] — a clean-looking Helio Start data point pulled toward launch/revenue language. Riley holding "readiness gate, not launch" keeps the beta-scope boundary from [[project_growth_gates_entitlement]] intact even as the numbers improve.

**How to apply:** Treat "readiness gate" and "launch" as distinct claims going forward — good rollup numbers can support the former, never the latter, until Riley/Priya explicitly say otherwise. Keep citing the four standing conditions (support-load, admin-proof, entitlement-instrumentation, unsupported-list) as the bar for Q1, not just the acceptance/workspace counts.

2023-12-22: Formal Q4 closeout meeting finalized the same Oct+Nov numbers (50 accepted, 34 admin-confirmed, 16 routed to CS pre-setup, 22 workspaces, 19 first integrations) and locked the accepted-scope statement going forward: Helio Start activates cleanly only for simple under-50-seat accounts with verified admin ownership, no manual billing, no import/migration need, and a first-week integration path — anything outside that stays explicitly unsupported. Tomás's approval was explicit and narrow: a January readiness review with defined criteria, and nothing else — not GA, GA planning, pricing-page exposure, paid acquisition, broader beta exposure, or any public launch commitment. Marcus accepted (without the pushback seen in prior rounds, see [[project_q4_forecast_helio_narrative]]) that there is no Q4 launch forecast, forecastable pipeline, or revenue-channel language to claim. Broader exposure stays blocked until the admin/permissions path stops generating avoidable CS handoffs.

January ownership split set at this meeting: Riley owns the operating model across eligibility, measurement, lifecycle, support load, and executive language (explicitly an operating-model role, not a formal new team); Owen owns the beta dashboard plus activation/support-load readout; Daniela owns entitlement/support-state instrumentation; Ines owns lifecycle copy and risk boundaries; Customer Success owns the routed-before-setup support paths.

**Why:** Closes out the Q4 controlled-beta phase with an explicit narrow-scope definition instead of letting good numbers imply readiness to widen — same discipline as the 12-15 entry above, now formalized with Tomás's specific non-approval list and a named January ownership matrix.

**How to apply:** For any January readiness-review work, treat the five-part eligibility definition (under-50 seats, verified admin, no manual billing, no import/migration, first-week integration) as the accepted starting scope, and route eligibility/measurement/lifecycle/support-load/exec-language questions to Riley while deferring dashboard specifics to Owen, instrumentation to Daniela, and lifecycle copy to Ines. Any ask to widen exposure before the admin-path support-handoff rate improves should be treated as out of scope, consistent with Tomás's explicit non-approval list.

Priya is explicitly unresolved on whether the three-cohort requirement also needs a minimum mature-account count per cohort — this is an open question, not yet a threshold, and should be flagged as unresolved rather than answered.

On 2024-04-07, while reviewing the continuation-gate draft, a hybrid threshold was proposed to resolve the open mature-account-floor question: at least three weekly cohorts totaling at least 150 admitted accounts with complete day-7 windows. This replaces a bare cohort-count with a size-aware bar so three small cohorts can't satisfy the gate on count alone. All other continuation criteria are retained unchanged: ordinary support coverage, zero refusal-boundary crossings, stable entitlement/lifecycle behavior, and the exclusions on mature conversion, retention, revenue, and forecastable pipeline language.

On 2024-04-08, Priya approved this hybrid threshold without revision: three mature weekly cohorts **and** at least 150 admitted accounts with complete day-7 windows, both parts required — if cohort three lands at 148, the gate waits rather than rounding up or letting cohort count substitute for the account floor. This approval covers only the review threshold itself; it is **not** a continuation decision, and not an expansion or pipeline-language approval. Support coverage, refusal-boundary crossings, routing, entitlement, and lifecycle remain separate checks, tracked independently of this threshold.

**Why:** Priya wants to avoid a single strong cohort ([[project_helio_start_first_mature_cohort_read]]) or bounded-GA success being read as automatic license to widen eligibility or scale acquisition, echoing the existing standing rule to wait for stabilization ([[feedback_stabilization_cohort]]) and to keep beta/GA data framed narrowly ([[feedback_beta_chart_framing]]). The hybrid threshold specifically addressed her unresolved concern that three cohorts could represent very different amounts of evidence depending on cohort size, and is now settled as the approved gate for review.

**How to apply:** When drafting or updating the continuation-gate brief or any related readout, treat three mature cohorts **and** ≥150 admitted accounts with complete day-7 windows as the approved review threshold (both required, no rounding or substituting one for the other). Keep support coverage, refusal-boundary crossings, routing, entitlement, and lifecycle as separate, independently-tracked checks rather than folding them into this threshold. Continue excluding continuation, expansion, and forecastable pipeline language from this brief — approval of the threshold is not approval of any of those.

On 2025-07-22 at 9:40am Central, Customer Success left two comments on the Helio Start internal triage FAQ:
1. "Pending assistance sounds like the workspace may already be admitted."
2. "Supported admission could be read as automatic after one successful check rather than after all required checks."

Both flag real ambiguity, not just wording nitpicks. Correction given: (1) "pending assistance" and "admitted" are distinct states — an account pending assistance has not completed the flow and is not admitted until it clears the required checks; the FAQ should say so explicitly. **Why:** Same underlying risk as the recurring "admitted" scope-precision issues ([[project_helio_start_q3_forecast_pipeline_question_jul2025]], [[project_cs_tooltip_authority_outreach_conflation_apr2025]]) — "admitted" keeps getting read as a stronger/looser signal than its actual definition (all required checks passed via the bounded organic path), so any customer- or CS-facing copy needs to guard against that drift precisely.

**How to apply:** When the FAQ is rewritten, confirm it explicitly distinguishes pending-assistance (not admitted) from admitted (all required checks passed, not just one), and avoid phrasing like "supported admission" that reads as automatic/single-check. Treat this the same as the CS tooltip authority/outreach conflation precedent — fix the copy, don't just clarify verbally.

On 2024-11-21, Owen found 7 workspaces in a secondary conversion-timing analysis with negative signup-to-first-paid lags. All 7 migrated from an older billing system; the imported legacy invoice date predates the Helio signup timestamp, even though signup and activation-v3 records are valid for all 7. A first Helio invoice timestamp is already available for 2 of the 7; finance-source timestamps are still outstanding for the other 5.

Interim treatment decided:
- The legacy migration invoice date is never substituted as the effective first-paid timestamp for lag purposes — it's a migration artifact, not an observed payment event.
- Activation counts are untouched: all 7 keep their activation-v3 classification and stay in the activation denominator, since signup and activation-v3 records are independently valid ([[project_activation_definition_v3]]).
- The 5 rows with no finance-source timestamp are excluded from the signup-to-first-paid lag distribution entirely, pending retrieval — no zero, no backfill, no migration-date substitute.
- The 2 rows with an available first Helio invoice timestamp are held as provisional, not folded into the reported lag distribution as validated observed values, until Finance confirms that timestamp is the true first-paid event.
- No partial/blended lag figure is computed or published for these 7 using whatever's available now; the existing closed day-30/day-90 tables in [[project_helio_start_first_paid_measurement_audit]] are not reopened or restated by this finding — if surfaced, it's a new, separately dated diagnostic line.

Audit note structure specified for Owen: list all 7 workspace IDs flagged as legacy-migration billing source artifacts; state explicitly that activation-v3 is unaffected and all 7 remain in activation counts; state explicitly that the migration date must never be used as the effective first-paid timestamp; per-row status (2 "provisional pending Finance confirmation", 5 "excluded pending finance-source timestamp retrieval"); and a note that resolution updates the lag distribution as a dated event, not a silent revision.

**Why:** Same fail-closed logic as [[project_helio_start_connector_log_latency_timestamp_exclusion]] (never substitute an artifact timestamp for a missing real one) and [[feedback_interim_maturity_no_early_call]] (never present an incomplete/partial read as if it were the observed result). User explicitly ruled out migration-date substitution, activation exclusion, and presenting incomplete timing as observed lag.

**How to apply:** For any future Helio Start timing/lag metric affected by legacy-migration data quality, apply this same three-part pattern: exclude rows lacking a real source timestamp from the specific timing metric only, never touch activation-v3 or other independently-valid classifications, and treat any single available-but-unconfirmed timestamp as provisional until source-validated.

**Update (2024-11-26):** Finance retrieved first-Helio-invoice timestamps for 4 of the 5 outstanding rows. Combined with the 2 previously-provisional rows (now finance-confirmed), 6 of 7 workspaces have valid signup-to-first-Helio-invoice intervals: MIG-01 3.0d, MIG-02 3.0d, MIG-03 0.5d, MIG-04 3.0d, MIG-05 1.5d, MIG-06 1.5d — interim median 2.25 days (n=6). **Final update (2024-12-02) — CLOSED:** Finance supplied the last outstanding timestamp for MIG-07 (signup 10/6 10:00am CT → first Helio invoice 10/8 10:00am CT = 48h/2.0d). All 7 workspaces now finance-confirmed. Final distribution (n=7): MIG-03 12h, MIG-05 36h, MIG-06 36h, MIG-07 48h, MIG-01 72h, MIG-02 72h, MIG-04 72h.
