metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: project
  originSessionId: d04a6e67-83ee-48ba-9f55-22d97eb6399a
  modified: 2026-09-19T00:47:09.070Z
---

On 2024-08-02, at the operating discussion closing out the continuation gate's evidence bar, the user presented the complete day-90 status table ([[project_helio_start_first_paid_measurement_audit]]): 39 paid-active, 7 canceled, 4 past due, 2 billing hold (all 52 admitted workspaces mature). Priya and Tomás agreed this is evidence that bounded organic Helio Start operates as a real product motion. The user declined Marcus Vail's request to turn the 39 paid-active workspaces into a Q3 paid-acquisition or pipeline claim, on the grounds that 13 of 52 were not paid-and-active at day 90, the cohort came entirely through the organic pricing-page path, and no acquisition-cost comparison exists. Priya and Tomás confirmed Helio Start remains an organic bounded channel through Q3.

The meeting also set a forward evidence bar: any future paid-acquisition proposal for Helio Start must combine (1) mature day-90 retention status, (2) refund-adjusted cash, and (3) account-level support effort — not rely on first-paid, activation, or paid-active status alone. Owen and Customer Success were assigned ownership of producing that combined evidence.

**Why:** This is the second time Marcus has pushed to attach pipeline/expansion language to evidence not built for it ([[project_helio_start_continuation_gate_outcome]], [[project_marcus_vail_postmortem]], [[project_expansion_mrr_concentration_feb2024]]), and completing the day-90 evidence bar did not automatically reopen the paid-acquisition door — a new, more specific bar was set instead of treating single-metric evidence (like 39/52 paid-active) as sufficient.

**How to apply:** Keep Helio Start framed as organic-only through Q3 ([[project_helio_start_continuation_gate_outcome]], [[feedback_riley_mrr_snapshot_framing]], [[feedback_planning_revenue_framing]]). If a paid-acquisition or Q3 pipeline proposal resurfaces, check whether it combines all three required elements (retention status, refund-adjusted cash, account-level support effort) with Owen/CS as the producing owners — a proposal built on only one of these (e.g. paid-active count alone) does not meet the bar and should be declined the same way this one was. Also watch for Marcus reframing a revenue/retention figure (e.g. cash-per-workspace) as if it were a cost figure (CAC) — that's a category error distinct from the "insufficient evidence" objection, and needs to be named as such rather than just re-asserting the three-part bar.

On 2024-08-14, Owen delivered the completed account-level join for all 52 mature workspaces, closing out all three legs: refund-adjusted cash through Aug 9 is $18,960 (three later refunds assigned to their workspaces); 31/52 workspaces have zero post-admission product-support minutes, 21/52 have ≥1 contact totaling 684 minutes ([[project_helio_start_support_load_classification]] three-bucket split). This satisfies the agreed matching requirement but still does not enable a paid-acquisition claim: the organic cohort has no paid-channel cost or conversion comparison, so no unit economics for a paid channel can be derived from it. The bar is complete for describing the organic cohort's own performance, not for justifying a paid-acquisition proposal.

On 2024-08-19, Marcus made a third attempt: dividing the $18,960 refund-adjusted cash by 52 workspaces ($364.62) and proposing to call it an "allowable paid-acquisition CAC." The user rejected this on the grounds that it's a category error, not just an insufficient-evidence issue — the figure is average organic cash generated per workspace (a revenue/retention number), not a cost of acquisition (there is no acquisition spend in this cohort to divide by anything). Even as a hypothetical spend ceiling, there is no paid-channel cost, acquisition mix, or paid-vs-organic response data to benchmark it against.

On 2024-09-12, Owen and CS delivered the combined worksheet for the next acquisition discussion, updating the figures: settled cash $18,960 minus $1,140 in later refunds = $17,820 refund-adjusted cash (previously $18,960 was itself already called "refund-adjusted" on 8-14 before this later refund landed — watch for stale citations of the $18,960 figure). Support effort was also broken out further: of the 21/52 contacted workspaces, 8 are high-effort (472 of 684 total minutes, 69%) and 13 are lower-effort (212 minutes); 31/52 remain zero-contact. Same limits applied: per-workspace cash ($342.69 all-cohort or $456.92 per-paid-active) is a revenue/retention figure, not a cost, so it cannot become a CAC or allowable-spend figure; the 8-workspace concentration is a descriptive distributional finding, not a basis for a staffing ratio, since there's no data on whether this subgroup is representative of a scaled/paid cohort or what a support-minute costs.

On 2025-08-05, per the reuse of this same 52-workspace mature day-90 table in the 2025-07-30 month-end packet ([[feedback_month_end_packet_evidence_reuse_framing]]), Customer Success delivered a fresh account-level support-effort cut, this time partitioned by contact count rather than minute-threshold: 31/52 had no post-admission support contact (consistent with prior zero-contact counts), 15/52 had exactly one ordinary integration question (median 16 minutes), and 6/52 had two or more contacts (median 41 minutes) — 21/52 contacted in total, matching the prior 8-high/13-low split's combined count even though the two cuts partition the same 21 workspaces differently (by minutes vs. by contact count). No admitted workspace required manual billing, import, or migration work. Refund-adjusted cash for this packet has not yet arrived, so the evidence bar's cash leg remains outstanding as of this date.

On 2024-09-20, Marcus Vail asked the user to treat a proposed $12,000 October media test as committed forecast spend, on the grounds that the mature Helio Start retention/refund-adjusted-cash/support-effort worksheet ([[project_helio_start_paid_acquisition_evidence_bar_aug2024]], completed 2024-09-12) now exists. The user declined via private Slack, distinguishing "having the required operating evidence" from "having an approved paid-channel experiment, a forecast commitment, or an allowable CAC." Reasons given: no expected paid-activation count exists (no paid-traffic response data to project from), no paid-cohort refund/support model exists (current figures describe the organic cohort only), and the worksheet's per-workspace cash figure is revenue/retention, not cost, so it still can't derive a CAC or spend ceiling. Helio Start remains organic-only through end of Q3.

**Why:** This is at least the fourth distinct attempt by Marcus to convert Helio Start operating evidence into paid-acquisition/forecast permission — first the continuation-gate pipeline target (5-24-24), then the 39/52 paid-active figure (8-2-24), then reframing refund-adjusted cash as CAC (8-19-24), now reframing "evidence bar met" as "test approved, spend committed." Each attempt uses newly-completed evidence as the leverage point, so completing evidence work does not itself close this pattern — a new framing keeps appearing at each new evidence milestone.

**How to apply:** Continue applying [[project_helio_start_paid_acquisition_evidence_bar_aug2024]]'s three-part bar test, but also watch specifically for the "evidence exists → therefore proposal is approved/committed" leap, which is a distinct move from citing a single insufficient metric. 2024-10-10: Owen flagged an ambiguity in the prospective Helio Start diagnostic ([[project_owen_workspace_manual_review_sep2024]]) using workspace HS-014 as the example: Agent A active 13:10–13:40 (30 min), Agent B active 13:20–13:35 (15 min, fully overlapping A), customer-blocked elapsed interval 13:10–13:40 (30 min), exported sum of agent time 45 min. Summed agent minutes overstate the customer's actual wait when agents work concurrently.

2024-10-15: Owen and Customer Success resolved the ambiguity. Final data-dictionary definitions (no longer interim):
- **Summed human agent-minutes:** total minutes of active work performed by human agents, summed across agents. Concurrent work counts each agent's labor, so overlapping agents contribute their minutes separately. Automated acknowledgements contribute zero.
- **Elapsed customer-blocked time:** the elapsed duration of the customer-blocking interval, recorded separately from human labor. Not substituted for or combined with agent-minutes. Automated acknowledgements contribute zero.

For HS-014, the measures remain 45 agent-minutes and 30 elapsed blocked minutes.

**Why:** A single blended "support minutes" figure would double-count overlap time and conflate customer-experienced wait with internal labor cost — same anti-collapsing principle as [[feedback_day90_status_table_framing]] and the full-cohort vs. contacted-only dual-average rule in [[project_helio_start_support_load_classification]].

**How to apply:** For the 60-workspace prospective diagnostic (and any workspace within it showing multi-agent overlap), report elapsed and summed-agent figures separately with these exact definitions and labels rather than publishing one merged number. The diagnostic's admission and routing rules are unchanged.

QA flagged 2 events in the access/authority group as possibly automated acknowledgements rather than real contacts.

**Rule defined:** A "contact" counts toward repeat-contact only if it's a substantive two-way interaction (customer-initiated message/reply, or an agent reply requiring customer action or advancing resolution). System-generated automated acknowledgements (ticket-received notices, auto-replies, status-change pings) are excluded — they reflect tooling, not support effort, mirroring the effort-vs-noise split already used for billing contacts in [[project_helio_start_support_load_classification]].

**Why:** Counting automated events as contacts would inflate the repeat-contact metric for whichever group happens to generate more automated tooling noise, without reflecting actual customer friction — undermining the diagnostic's purpose of comparing real support burden by mechanism.

**How to apply:** QA must audit all 8 workspace rows for automated events, not only the 2 already flagged in the access/authority group — auditing one group asymmetrically would bias the comparison. Report both raw preliminary counts and automation-adjusted counts side by side. Do not change the 8-workspace cohort, the 472-min total, mechanism-group membership, the accepted 52-workspace denominator, mature day-90 statuses, or the pre-admission/billing exclusions. Given group sizes of n=4/3/1, treat any adjusted-count comparison as descriptive/directional only — no percentages or "X group takes longer" conclusions — consistent with the diagnostic-not-decision framing already set for this review.

**Worked example (2024-10-03):** A support sequence with an automated ack, an agent question asking when the org owner will be available, the customer's reply that the owner is out until Thursday, and a closing "Thanks, I'll keep this open" — nets to 2 substantive contacts. The automated ack is excluded per the rule above. The agent's question counts (it requests new information / advances resolution). The customer's answer counts (it supplies new information). The closing courtesy message does not count — it carries no new substantive content, just status/acknowledgement, and should be treated the same as an automated ack for counting purposes even though a human wrote it.

name: project_helio_start_support_load_classification
description: Rule for splitting Helio Start support contacts between admitted support load vs pre-admission eligibility/ownership queue
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: project
  originSessionId: 1292dc8e-3119-4465-8fb4-710eaab0f5a3
  modified: 2026-09-17T17:01:16.544Z
---

Support contacts tied to Helio Start applicants must be split by admission status before counting toward admitted support load: ordinary integration questions from already-admitted workspaces count; contacts occurring *before* admission concerning eligibility/ownership evidence do not — those belong in a pre-admission review/routing queue instead.

**Why:** On the Apr 1–3, 2024 slice (16 contacts: 12 admitted-workspace integration questions, 4 pre-admission eligibility/ownership cases), the draft dashboard lumped all 16 into admitted support load, which would inflate that metric and mischaracterize eligibility-stage friction as post-admission support burden. Consistent with [[project_owen_helio_start_reporting_spec_fix_mar2024]] (support load measured against eligible/admitted starts) and [[project_cs_runbook_tabletop_fix_mar2024]] (pending-proof/ownership routing cases).

**How to apply:** When Helio Start support counts are reported, check admission timing per contact before bucketing. The Apr 1–3, 2024 slice was validated by Owen and CS on 2024-04-04: 12 admitted-workspace contacts = 10 distinct workspaces (ordinary integration questions, count toward admitted support load); 4 pre-admission contacts = 4 distinct applicants (eligibility/ownership evidence, excluded). No case crossed the published admission boundary. The raw total of 16 must not be reused as admitted support load.

On 2024-08-06, CS delivered the first account-level support export for the mature 52-workspace cohort (workspace ID, contact date, contact type, handling minutes), needed as the "account-level support effort" leg of [[project_helio_start_paid_acquisition_evidence_bar_aug2024]]. The two-way admission-timing split was extended to three buckets: (1) pre-admission assistance (eligibility/ownership/connector-credential contacts before admission_date — excluded, same rule as above; 11 such contacts were mixed into this export); (2) post-admission product support (ordinary integration/usage contacts after admission_date — this is the support-effort figure Owen joins to refund-adjusted cash); (3) billing contacts (payment/refund/invoice-related, any timing — tracked separately and NOT summed into support-effort minutes, since they're a proxy for the cash leg, not product friction, and blending them would undercut having two independent evidence legs). Zero-contact workspaces are NOT dropped: the denominator is the full mature 52-workspace roster from [[project_helio_start_first_paid_measurement_audit]], left-joined to cleaned support minutes with missing rows treated as 0 contacts, consistent with the denominator-first practice in [[feedback_day90_status_table_framing]].

On 2024-08-20, the validated post-admission product-support figure from this export was computed as 684 minutes total across the 52 mature workspaces: 31 workspaces with zero post-admission contacts, 21 with at least one. Two averages must both be shown, never just one: full-cohort average = 684/52 ≈ 13.15 min/workspace (overall support burden including zero-contact workspaces); contacted-only average = 684/21 ≈ 32.57 min/workspace (support intensity conditional on having a contact). Reporting only the 21-workspace average overstates cohort-wide burden; reporting only the 52-workspace average hides how concentrated the effort is among contacted workspaces. Pre-admission connector assistance and billing contacts remain excluded from both figures, per the three-bucket split above.

Ines's draft Q1 goal framed all preflight/governed-send holds as something to drive toward zero. That's wrong: holds triggered by missing/conflicting state, stale external-authority timestamps, or conflicting CS-work status are the fail-closed control working as designed (see [[project_expansion_assist_freshness_failclosed_rule]], [[project_helio_start_maintenance_window_failclosed_precedent]]), not errors to eliminate.

Rewritten goal (2025-02-07): Ines owns release-time consumption of the shared lifecycle state contract (see [[project_lifecycle_state_contract_settled_feb2025]]) for routine, non-state-changing sends within her standing authority (cap ≤3 sends/week, no engineering release access — see [[project_ines_lifecycle_ownership_trial_oct2024]]). Measured by:
1. 100% of governed sends audited within the 24-hour window, no lapses.
2. Zero unsupported releases — every released row had current/supported state at send time.
3. Every held/exception row gets a fresh current-state re-check before any later release; no retroactive approval of a previously-held row.
4. Hold volume/category tracked as a diagnostic (per the 4-category taxonomy in [[project_owen_lifecycle_exception_taxonomy_feb2025]]), not as a defect metric to minimize.

Explicit non-goal: reducing hold count is not a target. A correct hold is success, not failure.

**Why:** Ines's role is judgment over message-state consumption plus routine release authority already earned through a clean trial ([[project_ines_lifecycle_ownership_trial_oct2024]]) — a goal that rewards fewer holds would incentivize pushing through unsupported releases, undermining the fail-closed discipline built up across [[project_expansion_assist_freshness_failclosed_rule]] and related incidents.

**How to apply:** When reviewing Ines's goals, scorecards, or performance narratives, check that hold/exception counts are never framed as negative outcomes on their own — only audit completeness, correct classification, and absence of unsupported releases should be scored.

---

Owen asked (8-4-25) whether a future pre-breach warning should be added as another hold row when the same scheduled decision is later re-evaluated, or retained only as linked audit metadata. Ruling: every scheduled decision appears exactly once in the unique-decision denominator and carries one final disposition. A pre-breach warning is linked audit history, not another decision or hold row. If the decision later receives a field-specific hold, the warning, the hold, any fresh checks, and any reevaluations all stay linked to that same single decision without creating an additional denominator row.

**Why:** Keeps the Lifecycle Systems decision/hold counts (e.g., the 914 decisions/38 holds reported in the [[project_lifecycle_systems_arc]] Q3 operating review) from being inflated by re-touches of the same decision — consistent with the denominator-first discipline already used elsewhere (see [[feedback_interim_maturity_no_early_call]], [[feedback_day90_status_table_framing]]).

**How to apply:** When reviewing or reporting Lifecycle Systems decision/hold metrics, verify counts are per unique scheduled decision, not per event touching that decision. Pre-breach warnings, holds, fresh checks, and reevaluations for the same decision should be traceable via linkage, never tallied as separate rows.

**2026-09-19 update:** This rule was written into the July 31 Q3 evidence-lock template, including an explicit guard against counting one scheduled decision both as a pre-breach alert and as an additional hold or decision row. The template states this is a measurement/counting rule only — it does not assert or assume the source-age alert ([[project_lifecycle_source_age_alert_release_prep_checklist_jul2025]]) is live or effective in production; that is a separate, unaddressed question.

**8-19-25 update:** A second operator-guidance intervention was added to the same Q3 evidence-lock template, alongside the first (8-13-25): Ines independently caught a second CS-facing draft before it reached operators, correcting the same authority≠outreach conflation ("once external authority is verified, setup reminders are authorized across the account") — see [[project_cs_auto_nudge_arc]]. The entry is authored by Ines, as was the first. Adding it does not change anyone's authority: the user's exception/stop authority, Ines's independently-owned operator-guidance lane, and Daniela's engineering release and rollback control all remain exactly as they were. The template still does not resolve or anticipate the open September 24, 2025 decision on whether Ines's messaging-state review/operator-guidance lane becomes fully independent (see [[project_lifecycle_q3_close_review_sept2025]]) — this is evidence added ahead of the 9-19-25 lock, not a decision.

On 2025-02-04, Priya approved using the available two-engineer-day slot (Daniela's team) to build an operator-visible freshness alarm for the lifecycle-export pipeline. Scope: detect divergence between the source and consumer as-of times, and show both timestamps to the operator.

Explicitly deferred/out of scope:
- The cosmetic exception-card revision is deferred, not part of this slot.
- Approval does not authorize changing source semantics.
- Approval does not authorize overriding held rows.
- Approval does not authorize representing the shared state contract as live (it remains not-live per [[project_lifecycle_systems_charter_approved]]).

**Why:** Follows directly from the [[project_lifecycle_export_delay_refresh_incident_jan2025]] delayed-export incident (1-30-25), which exposed the gap this alarm addresses — operators had no visibility into source/consumer staleness before the fresh recheck was manually triggered.

**How to apply:** When tracking Daniela's team's engineering time or reviewing the freshness-alarm build, hold to this narrow scope — flag if work drifts into source semantics changes, override mechanisms, or exception-card cosmetics, since those were explicitly not approved in this slot.

**Prototype thresholds (Daniela, 2025-02-05):** export refresh target is hourly; warning fires when consumer timestamp lags source by >2 hours; critical fires at >4 hours lag. Both timestamps are displayed to the operator. Confirmed explicitly: alerting is display/notification only — it does not change eligibility and does not release held rows, consistent with the fail-closed precedent in [[project_helio_start_maintenance_window_failclosed_precedent]].

**Staging demonstration (Daniela, 2025-02-12):** confirmed thresholds behaviorally (warning at 2hr lag, critical at 4hr lag, both timestamps shown). New detail: once the source/consumer gap catches up, the banner does not auto-clear — it stays in the critical state until the operator manually refreshes the page. Worth flagging if this causes operator confusion once the alarm ships, since a stale-looking critical banner could be mistaken for an unresolved lag.

**Auto-clear + audit-history acceptance criteria (specified 2025-02-12, fixes the stuck-banner bug above):** Banner must auto-transition (critical→warning→cleared) once a subsequent check finds lag at/below threshold, re-evaluating live timestamps each check rather than assuming monotonic recovery; require 2 consecutive under-threshold checks before clearing to avoid flapping (N to be confirmed with Daniela against real check cadence). Clearing is display-only — it must never trigger or imply eligibility/suppression re-evaluation or release held rows; rows still require the manual recheck-against-fresh-data process from [[project_lifecycle_export_delay_refresh_incident_jan2025]]. Every state transition (none/warning/critical/cleared) is logged append-only with transition timestamp, source as-of, consumer as-of, and computed lag, visible to Ines/Owen; the audit view is read-only with no release/override action reachable from it, and a "cleared" entry documents display catch-up only, never row-level revalidation.

**Staging retest confirming auto-recovery fix (Daniela, 2025-02-17):** Warning/critical still fire at the approved 2hr/4hr thresholds; both source and consumer timestamps remain visible; the banner now clears automatically after a verified catch-up (per the 2-12-25 acceptance criteria above), resolving the stuck-banner bug. Held rows still stay held until their consumers perform fresh checks — auto-clear did not touch release logic. Alarm is active in staging only; the shared state contract remains not live in production.

**Production enablement + controlled verification (Daniela, 2026-02-20):** Alarm is now live in production for the existing lifecycle export — separate from the still-not-live shared-state feed. A controlled timestamp freeze test reproduced the approved 2hr warning / 4hr critical thresholds, displayed both source and consumer as-of times, and auto-cleared after verified catch-up per the 2-12-25 acceptance criteria; the incident interval is retained in the audit view. Held rows still require each consumer to perform a fresh check before release, and the alarm still has no authority to alter eligibility or release held rows — production behavior matches staging exactly, no scope drift.

On 2025-02-14, during a nonproduction shared-state replay, Helio Start reporting and Expansion Assist selection were confirmed to preserve the entitlement source timestamp in UTC, but lifecycle preflight was found to parse six entitlement updates as local time and place them on the prior Central calendar date. Current field values still matched across all three consumers, but as-of ordering and freshness evaluation differed between lifecycle preflight and the other two consumers. No production surface changed.

**Why:** This is a cross-consumer agreement gap in the same category the [[project_lifecycle_state_contract_shadow_replay_acceptance_criteria]] were designed to catch — value agreement alone is not sufficient if as-of/freshness timestamps disagree, since freshness evaluation drives the fail-closed hold behavior from [[project_lifecycle_state_contract_implementation_session_feb10_2025]]. It's the same class of bug as the Expansion Assist [[project_expansion_assist_timezone_window_classification_rule]] and the [[project_nov_signup_dashboard_warehouse_boundary_reconciliation_dec2024]] mismatch: comparing calendar-date/local-time renderings instead of absolute instants.

**How to apply:** Treat this as an open defect in lifecycle preflight's timestamp parsing, not a passed replay — even though the six records' values matched, they should not be described as in agreement, since as-of ordering and freshness differ. This sits alongside (not in place of) the fixture carry-forward defect from [[project_lifecycle_state_contract_fixture_test_jan_mismatch_feb2025]]; both must be resolved before shadow replay can be described as meeting its acceptance criteria. Fix should parse/compare entitlement timestamps as absolute UTC instants, consistent with the Expansion Assist precedent, not local calendar dates.

Correction/retest scope agreed 2025-02-14: (1) fix lifecycle preflight's timestamp parsing at the as-of/freshness computation layer (not just display), so it produces absolute-UTC-instant comparisons like the other two consumers; (2) retest must cover all five governed fields per [[project_lifecycle_state_contract_shadow_replay_acceptance_criteria]], not just the entitlement field where this was caught, and must include fail-closed/hold cases in case misparsing also shifts staleness triggers; (3) rerun stays nonproduction/shared-state until both this defect and the Jan fixture carry-forward defect are closed. Evidence must be worded as "shadow replay: FAILED — timestamp parsing inconsistent" with the affected consumer/field/record count named, not as "passed" or "mostly agreed"; field-value agreement is not sufficient grounds for a pass label per [[feedback_interim_maturity_no_early_call]] and [[feedback_day90_status_table_framing]]. No production surface is affected by this finding.

**Update 2025-02-18 — CLOSED:** Daniela changed the transformation to preserve the governed UTC source timestamp before applying Central-date display logic. Owen reran the nonproduction shadow replay and all three consumers now agree on values, event ordering, as-of times, and freshness outcomes; intentionally stale cases correctly remain held rather than inheriting prior eligibility. This closes the timezone-parsing defect. Still no production release approved or made — see [[project_lifecycle_preflight_clean_nonproduction_replay_no_release_feb2025]] for what remains before a release decision.

**Status: still open, nonproduction rehearsal only — not closed.**

On 2025-02-19, Daniela's first production runbook review (following the clean nonproduction replay, [[project_lifecycle_preflight_clean_nonproduction_replay_no_release_feb2025]]) found a rollback gap. The proposed kill switch stops new shared-state transport, but each consumer restores its prior authority independently and on a different path/timeline:
- Helio Start reporting: restores prior selector through the reporting deploy
- Expansion Assist: restores prior selection through the monthly-selection job
- Lifecycle preflight: restores prior source through Customer.io configuration

Because these restores are independent, one consumer could be back on the new shared-state feed while another is still on its old path for several minutes during a rollback. Daniela's draft states no assertion currently verifies all consumers return to the same authority at the same time.

**Why:** Matches the standing pattern for this contract ([[project_lifecycle_state_contract_shadow_replay_acceptance_criteria]], [[feedback_interim_maturity_no_early_call]]) — clean signals in one phase (replay) don't cover other release-readiness dimensions (rollback safety). A rollback gap during kill-switch use could put consumers in disagreement exactly during an incident, which is the scenario rollback exists to prevent.

**How to apply:** Treat this as an open defect blocking production release, separate from the shadow-replay acceptance criteria checklist. Before describing the contract as release-ready, confirm either (a) a cross-consumer rollback-synchronization assertion/check has been added and passed, or (b) this gap has been explicitly accepted/waived by a named owner.

**2025-02-19 decision:** user explicitly declined to approve a production replay pending this. Confirmed as a standalone release blocker, not covered by prior shadow-replay signoff. Next rehearsal must prove: (1) a tested, explicit max sync window across all three restore paths, not "eventually consistent"; (2) an active cross-consumer agreement check at end of rollback, same shape as steady-state; (3) all three restore paths exercised together in one run, not separately; (4) no customer-visible/hard-to-reverse action (e.g. Expansion Assist selection/messaging) taken by any consumer while it disagrees with the others during the transition; (5) fail-closed behavior during the disagreement window itself, not just steady state; (6) full timing/denominator evidence per path, not a collapsed pass/fail.

**2025-02-21 rehearsal (nonproduction):** Daniela replaced the three independent restore paths with one coordinated consumer-mode switch, backed by a preserved pre-replay selector snapshot, and rehearsed rollback in nonproduction. All three consumers (Helio Start reporting, Expansion Assist selection, lifecycle preflight) stopped reading the candidate feed and returned to their preserved selectors together, within 8 minutes. Synthetic missing/stale records stayed held (fail-closed intact); Owen verified no prior true eligibility value reappeared during the transition. No production replay or release occurred.

This addresses criteria (1) [tested max sync window, 8 min] and (3) [all three paths exercised together] from the 2-19 list, and is consistent with (5) [fail-closed during transition]. Still needs explicit confirmation against (2) active end-of-rollback agreement check, (4) no customer-visible action during disagreement window, and (6) full per-path timing/denominator evidence (not just the collapsed 8-minute figure) before this can be treated as closing the defect. Treat as progress, not resolution, until those are confirmed.

Ines completed a preliminary inventory (reported 2025-01-06) ahead of a January 15, 2025 contractor kickoff: 31 active lifecycle templates total — 18 routine non-state-changing, 8 state-changing, 5 exception-heavy. Six of the 18 routine templates lack a repeatable written suppression-check record.

Prioritization set for the contractor's first week (per [[project_ines_lifecycle_ownership_trial_oct2024]] boundaries — Ines's lasting authority covers only routine, non-state-changing sends):
1. Draft written suppression-check documentation for the 6 gap templates first (Ines reviews/signs off).
2. Extend the same documentation format to the other 12 routine templates for consistency.
3. State-changing (8) and exception-heavy (5) templates: documentation/cataloging only (logic, triggers, owners, known exceptions) — no suppression-check execution or release actions by the contractor.

State-changing and exception-heavy templates remain under the user's higher-risk authority and Daniela's engineering controls; the contractor's role is explicitly scoped to preparation and repeatability, not release-authority transfer. Planned check-in with the user at end of week 1 before any expansion of contractor scope.

Update (2025-01-10, ahead of kickoff): Ines finished the contractor prework inventory. Inventory total confirmed unchanged at 31 templates. The six routine templates still lack repeatable written suppression-check records (unresolved gap, matches 2025-01-06 count). New finding: 4 templates (not yet specified which tier) have no documented accountable campaign owner — a distinct gap from the suppression-check issue, to be catalogued (not resolved) during contractor week 1 per the prep-only scope above.

**Why:** Extends the routine/state-changing authority split already established for Ines ([[project_ines_lifecycle_ownership_trial_oct2024]]) to a new contractor role — the risk is scope creep from "documentation help" into de facto release authority if not bounded explicitly up front.
**How to apply:** Any future request to expand contractor scope (e.g., touching state-changing/exception-heavy templates beyond cataloging, or contractor executing suppression checks) should be flagged as a boundary change requiring explicit approval, not an incremental extension of week 1 prep work.

**Update (2025-01-15, kickoff day):** Contractor asked whether resolving the four campaign-owner gaps and six suppression-check gaps means assigning owners and approving the records. Answer given: no — contractor inventories evidence, identifies missing records/owners, and drafts checklists/documentation in the standard format, but does not assign campaign ownership, does not approve/certify suppression-check records as final, and does not inherit Ines's, Riley's, or Daniela's decision rights. Ines retains sign-off on suppression-check records per the original week-1 plan; owner-assignment for the four gap templates stays with whoever already holds ownership authority in that domain, not the contractor.

**Update (2025-01-17):** Found a likely tier-mismatch in the contractor's flow inventory: the "Account-status summary" template is labeled "routine education" (implying the 18-template non-state-changing tier), but its release behavior writes `status_summary_sent_at` and advances the recipient into the follow-up branch — hallmarks of the 8-template state-changing tier. Flagged to user, not yet resolved with Ines/contractor as of this update. If mislabeled templates like this go untagged, they risk being swept into the contractor's routine-tier suppression-check documentation (or Ines's sign-off track) instead of staying under the user's/Daniela's higher-risk, cataloging-only scope.

**Update (2025-01-17, later same day — reclassification and authority split):** Account-status summary confirmed reclassified from the 18-template routine/non-state-changing tier to the 8-template state-changing tier (writes `status_summary_sent_at`, advances recipient into follow-up branch). This moves it outside Ines's [[project_ines_lifecycle_ownership_trial_oct2024]] lasting authority (routine/non-state-changing only) and outside the contractor's scope (documentation/cataloging only, no suppression-check execution or release). Held audience stays held. Authority split set:
- Contractor: may document the flow (logic, trigger, owner, known exception) in the state-changing catalog — no approval, no release, no suppression-check execution.
- Ines: owns the formal reclassification (moving it in the inventory from 18→8 tier) and must run a fresh state-changing-tier preflight before any release decision — current-state check (suppression, merge-alias, release metadata, connector state) plus explicit confirmation of the downstream follow-up-branch consequence, fail-closed on anything missing/conflicting. Completing this preflight does not carry release authority for this tier.
- Riley: holds the higher-risk release/approval decision for this now-state-changing template, consistent with the pattern that state-changing/ambiguous/exception-heavy sends require sign-off above Ines and the contractor.

**Note:** prior [[project_ines_lifecycle_ownership_trial_oct2024]] entries (2024-11-08 permanent grant) recorded "the user" as holding stop/state-changing decision authority, not Riley by name. This is the first instance naming Riley specifically as the higher-risk decision-holder for a lifecycle template boundary — worth confirming with the user whether this is a general handoff of that authority to Riley or specific to this template, next time a state-changing/exception-heavy send decision comes up.

**Update (2025-01-22):** Contractor asked Ines for a Customer.io export covering all 31 active templates with fields: template ID, recipient destination, suppression reason, current-state timestamp, campaign owner. This spans all three tiers (18 routine, 8 state-changing, 5 exception-heavy), and recipient destination + suppression reason + current-state timestamp are live per-recipient operational data, not the logic/trigger/owner documentation the contractor's scope covers for state-changing/exception-heavy templates. Not yet resolved as of this update — flag as a scope question (live data export vs. documentation/cataloging) before Ines fulfills it, especially for the 13 non-routine templates.

**Update (2025-01-22, boundary defined):** Resolved the export scope question by defining the dataset Ines should give the contractor as template-*definition*-level, not a live audience export:
- Include: template ID, tier, whether a written suppression-check record exists (and if not, which specific check type is missing, e.g. "no merge-alias check defined"), trigger/logic description, documented known exceptions, campaign owner field (populated, or flagged "no owner assigned" for the 4 gap templates).
- Exclude: recipient destination, per-recipient suppression reason, current-state timestamp — these are live per-recipient/release-time operational data, unnecessary for documenting whether a check exists and outside the contractor's no-suppression-check-execution, no-release scope.

**Why:** Keeps the contractor's access matched to "does a check exist and what does it check for" (documentation) rather than "what happened to this specific recipient" (live audience/release data), consistent with the 1-15-25 no-execution/no-release ruling and Ines's retained sign-off on actual suppression-check records.
**How to apply:** Any future data request from the contractor should be evaluated against this same split — template-definition/catalog fields are in scope, live per-recipient/audience/release-time fields are not, regardless of which tier the template falls in.

**Update (2025-01-30, reconstruction worksheet for the 6 gap templates):** Contractor's reconstruction worksheet on the six routine templates lacking suppression-check records found: 4 have archived release manifests plus timestamped audits proving the check occurred historically; 2 have no preserved release manifest or other contemporaneous proof. Current template configuration is available for all six, but current config does not prove what happened at the historical release — it can inform a documentation format going forward, not retroactively certify the missing 2. The 4 with archived proof can likely move to "documented, Ines sign-off pending" status; the 2 without proof remain a genuine gap needing a decision (e.g., accept as undocumented-historical / require a fresh forward-looking check) rather than being papered over with current-state config.

**Update (2025-02-03, post-engagement retention request — flagged, not approved):** With the engagement ending Feb 23, the contractor proposed retaining a downloadable personal "example pack" for future portfolio use, requesting: template identifiers, redacted example rows, suppression-check names, reconstructed evidence labels, current campaign-owner names, and internal folder paths. This is a different kind of request from anything granted so far — not an access-scope question during the engagement, but a permanent external export of internal artifacts (including colleagues' names and internal infra paths) for reuse outside the company after the engagement ends. Flagged to the user as needing explicit data-handling/policy sign-off (not a routine extension of the documentation scope) — not approved as of this update.

**Why:** The established boundary (1-22-25) governs what the contractor can *see* during the engagement (template-definition-level, no live/operational data); it doesn't address *permanent retention/export* by the contractor after the engagement ends, which is a materially different risk (data leaving company control indefinitely, employee names going external, no established redaction standard).
**How to apply:** Any future "can I keep a copy for my portfolio/reference" ask from a contractor or vendor should be treated as a distinct decision point requiring explicit data-handling/security sign-off, not folded into whatever access scope was already granted for the engagement itself.

**Update (2025-02-05, owner-gap return for the 4 campaign-owner gap templates):** Contractor returned findings on the 4 templates flagged 2025-01-10 as lacking a documented accountable campaign owner:
- Onboarding-help series: current release checklist names Ines as owner.
- Renewal reminder: current runbook names Customer Success operations as owner.
- Integration summary: no named owner found — only an old folder creator is available as a proxy signal.
- Trial-expiry education: no named owner found — only a recent editor is available as a proxy signal.

Two of the four (onboarding-help, renewal reminder) now have a plausible named owner surfaced from existing documentation. The other two (integration summary, trial-expiry education) remain genuine gaps — folder-creator and recent-editor are incidental metadata, not evidence of accountable ownership, and shouldn't be treated as resolving the gap.

**Why:** Matches the 1-15-25 kickoff-day ruling — the contractor inventories/surfaces evidence and drafts documentation but does not assign campaign ownership or approve/certify records; "who touched this file" is not the same as "who is the accountable owner."
**How to apply:** Treat onboarding-help and renewal reminder as candidate-owner findings needing confirmation by whoever holds assignment authority in that domain (not the contractor), and treat integration summary and trial-expiry education as still-open owner gaps until an actual accountable owner is assigned — don't let folder-creator/recent-editor metadata get reported upward as if it closed the gap.

**Update (2025-02-12, closeout inventory):** Ahead of the engagement's 2025-02-23 end date, the contractor's closeout inventory confirms: 31 active templates total, 29 with evidence-backed accountable owners. The remaining 2 — integration summary and trial-expiry education — still lack an approved owner; only an old folder creator or recent editor is available as a proxy signal, which per the 2-5-25 ruling does not resolve the gap. On suppression-check records, the closeout confirms the 1-30-25 reconstruction split unchanged: 4 of the 6 originally-missing records are reconstructable from archived manifests plus timestamped audits (still "documented, Ines sign-off pending," not yet certified); 2 have no contemporaneous proof and remain a genuine open gap needing an explicit decision.

**Why:** This is a status restatement at closeout, not new resolution — the same two owner gaps (2-5-25) and same two no-proof suppression-check gaps (1-30-25) persist unchanged into the final week of the engagement.
**How to apply:** Do not let the closeout inventory's "29/31 owned" or "4/6 reconstructed" framing read as full closure — flag to the user that 2 owner gaps and 2 suppression-check proof gaps require an actual decision (assign an owner; accept-as-undocumented vs. require a fresh forward check) before or independent of the contractor's 2-23-25 exit, since the contractor has no authority to resolve either.

**Update (2025-02-12, closeout priority order and evidence-safe labels set):** Priority order for the final week before the 2025-02-23 exit: (1) resolve the integration-summary and trial-expiry-education owner gaps via whoever actually holds assignment authority in that domain — not the contractor; (2) decide disposition of the 2 no-proof suppression-check gaps (accept-as-undocumented-historical vs. require a fresh forward-looking check) — a decision only Ines/the user can make; (3) route the 4 reconstructed suppression-check records to Ines for actual sign-off before exit, so they don't sit indefinitely in "pending"; (4) resolve (approve or decline) the 2-3-25 portfolio/export retention request, since it's a distinct data-handling decision separate from documentation scope.

Evidence-safe labels defined for the contractor's closeout deliverables:
- Integration summary: "Owner: unassigned — folder creator is incidental metadata, not ownership evidence."
- Trial-expiry education: "Owner: unassigned — recent editor is incidental metadata, not ownership evidence."
- The 4 reconstructable suppression checks: "Documented — reconstructed from archived release manifest + timestamped audit. Historical occurrence evidenced; not certified. Ines sign-off pending." (never "verified" or "closed" until Ines actually signs off.)
- The 2 no-proof suppression checks: "No contemporaneous evidence available — undocumented-historical, open gap. Current template configuration does not retroactively prove historical execution." (current-state config must not be cited as if it closes the gap.)

**Why:** Keeps the contractor's final deliverables from silently converting incidental metadata (folder-creator/recent-editor) or current-state config into implied ownership or certified status, consistent with the 1-15-25 no-assignment/no-certification ruling and the 2-5-25/1-30-25 findings.
**How to apply:** When reviewing the contractor's closeout artifacts, confirm owner and suppression-check fields use these exact evidentiary labels rather than being marked resolved/closed, and confirm all 4 open decision points (2 owner gaps, 2 no-proof gaps, 4 pending sign-offs, the retention request) get actual decisions from the people who hold that authority before or independent of the 2-23-25 exit — the contractor documents what the evidence shows, never assigns authority by inference.

**Update (2025-02-19, display-name collisions found in final inventory):** While checking the contractor's final 31-template inventory, Ines found three pairs of templates sharing an identical display name despite representing different campaign states, each with a distinct template ID and release history:
- "Setup reminder" — routine education template (18-tier) vs. a state-changing follow-up template (8-tier).

The "Integration summary" collision also touches the still-open integration-summary owner gap (2-5-25/2-12-25) — a retired 2024 template sharing that name could contaminate evidence gathered for the live owner-gap decision if not disambiguated by ID.
**How to apply:** Treat this as a distinct defect from the owner/suppression-check gaps — flag to the user/Ines that any inventory, documentation, or routing work referencing these three display names must key off template ID, not display name, until the collisions are resolved (e.g., renaming or retiring the stale/duplicate label) by whoever holds that production-identifier authority (not the contractor). Don't let this get folded into the existing owner-gap or suppression-check-gap closeout items — it's a naming/routing risk, not an ownership or evidence gap.

**Update (2025-02-21, access inventory ahead of exit):** Contractor access inventory confirms: read-only Customer.io access and Team-workspace commenter access are both active, with both scheduled to expire 2025-02-28 (five days after the 2-23-25 engagement end date). metadata:

  type: project
  originSessionId: d61df06a-d1b3-4a6b-b6eb-6b1016c530da
  modified: 2026-09-18T04:26:26.035Z
---

Onboarding-notice deduplication operates at the workspace level, not the normalized-destination-address level. Two different workspaces (e.g. North and Sandbox) that happen to share the same contact mailbox will each independently trigger their own onboarding notice — that is expected behavior, not a duplicate send.

**Why:** 11-5-24 Ines forwarded a customer report that `billing@ourco.com` (shared by North and Sandbox workspaces) received two onboarding emails same morning. Confirmed one delivery per workspace, no replay within either workspace — the rule doesn't dedup across workspaces by shared destination, only within a single workspace's own lifecycle.

**How to apply:** When investigating "duplicate" onboarding/notification reports, first check whether multiple workspace IDs are involved before assuming a dedup-rule violation. Don't describe cross-workspace sends to a shared mailbox as "duplicates" in customer-facing language — frame it as two workspaces sharing contact info. If the customer wants fewer emails, offer per-workspace suppression rather than implying a bug. Related: [[project_expansion_assist_exposure_counting_rule]] (similar acct-level dedup precedent, different product surface).

**Recommended fix (2026-09-18):** one primary row per unique scheduled decision (dedupe by scheduled-decision ID per [[project_cs_auto_nudge_scheduled_decision_duplicate_records_may2025]]), bucketed into mutually exclusive final outcomes — suppressed, proceeded, or still-held. Owen's daily first-paid chart showed 46 events on 2-27-24 vs a normal 18-24 range. Root cause: 17 historical January invoices (invoice_paid_at Jan 3-31) were replayed into the event stream during a billing backfill, landing with event_received_at of 2-27-24; the other 29 were genuine 2-27-24 first payments. No customer was double-charged.

Resolution: attribute the 17 backfilled records to their original invoice_paid_at (not ingestion date) for trend/alert purposes; add a source_type tag (billing_backfill vs live) rather than deleting/overwriting event_received_at, which stays intact for audit. Feb 27 chart shows 29 genuine first-paid; the 17 fold back into their original January days on recompute. Alert thresholds should key off invoice_paid_at-based series, not raw ingestion counts.

**Why:** keeps the audit trail fully intact (no deletion of raw records) while preventing a replay from misreading as an acquisition/conversion spike — consistent with the user's recurring approach of tagging/flagging rather than deleting, seen in [[project_daniela_instrumentation_fix_feb2024]] and [[project_dormant_automation_cleanup_feb2024]].

**How to apply:** for any future backfill or replayed event batch, recommend event-time (business date) attribution for reporting/alerting, preserve ingestion timestamp for audit, and use a source tag to distinguish replay from live events rather than overwriting or deleting anything.

**Status (2-28-24):** implemented — Owen switched the daily first-paid chart to invoice_paid_at, keeping event_received_at for pipeline monitoring. Feb 27 now shows 29 genuine first payments; the 17 Jan records remain tagged as the Feb 27 backfill in the audit trail. Monthly total unchanged, alert baseline reset, no billing impact. Closed.

Standing protocol for any Sam's dinner with an allergen-substitute plate, adopted 2024-06-03 after a near miss at the June 1 sesame-allergy dinner where a runner set a standard sesame-garnish tray next to two allergy-safe plates before Sam caught it.

**Why:** The substitute-glaze/dedicated-equipment plan handled kitchen prep but left expo-line spatial separation and garnish-access rules undefined, so a correctly prepared allergy plate still nearly ended up contaminated by proximity/handling at pass.

**How to apply:** For every remaining dinner with an allergen guest, confirm this sequence is in place before service:
1. **Plate placement** — allergy-safe plates are plated and staged in a fixed, physically separate zone of the pass (e.g., far end or a marked tray), never adjacent to standard-garnish trays.
2. **Labels** — allergy-safe plates get a visible marker (colored pick, ticket flag, or plate ring) placed the moment they're plated, kept on until the server picks up.
3. **Who may garnish** — only the chef or Sam garnishes near/around allergy-safe plates; line cooks and runners are barred from touching or setting anything (including allergen garnish trays) in that staging zone.
4. **Final verbal handoff** — before a server takes an allergy-safe plate, Sam or chef gives an explicit verbal call-out naming the allergen and confirming the plate is clean, and the server repeats it back before carrying it out.

Related to [[project_sam_june1_sesame_allergy_dinner]] (the event that surfaced this gap) and [[project_sam_roasted_chicken_special]] (chef-owner approval dynamic for special dishes).

On 2024-05-23, the chef-owner reviewed full run economics for a roasted-chicken special Sam had run and declined to repeat it as-is: the current version needed three extra staff-hours, which the chef found too costly. Food and sales results were promising enough that Sam may propose another run, but only after designing and testing a batch plan that needs no more than one incremental staff-hour. No repeat date is approved.

On 2024-06-05, Sam kitchen-tested a revised batch plan (pre-staged marinade, changed tray sequence, same 30lb raw case): labor came in at 58 min (under the 1hr ceiling), yielding 43 seven-oz portions from 19.1 cooked lbs vs. the original run's 44 portions from 19.6 cooked lbs. This is one isolated kitchen-only trial, not tested under live-service conditions, with no sell-through data yet.

On 2024-06-11 (Sunday prep window), Sam ran a second batch test of the same revised sequence (same 30lb raw case, no deviations noted from the pre-staging/tray plan): 59 incremental min (under the 1hr ceiling), yielding 19.5 cooked lbs / 312 oz → 44 complete 7-oz portions with 4 oz left over. This meets both chef-owner thresholds (≤60 incremental min, ≥44 complete portions) and Sam submitted the result to the chef-owner.

On 2024-06-17, the chef-owner approved one additional sale run for Friday, 2024-06-28, based on the two passing tests. Conditions: must use the tested pre-staging/tray sequence, stay at or below 60 incremental staff minutes, and target at least 44 seven-oz portions. Sam must record actual cooked yield, labor, sales, and unsold portions from that run before the chef-owner will consider any further repeat. This is approval for one sale run only — not an ongoing menu addition or any change to Sam's role.

On 2024-06-28, Sam ran the approved sale run using the tested pre-staging/tray sequence, no deviations noted. From the 30lb raw case: 19lb 12oz (316oz) cooked yield → 45 complete 7-oz portions with 1oz left over; incremental labor 57 min. Both thresholds met: 57 min ≤ 60-min ceiling, 45 portions ≥ 44-portion target. Of the 45 plated portions, 43 sold at $18 each (revenue $774); the remaining 2 were chilled for staff meal per food-handling procedure, not sold or wasted. Food cost $146; labor cost at $24/hr = $22.80; contribution (revenue − food cost − labor cost) = $605.20. Results reported to the chef-owner per the 6-17-24 condition. This closes the approved one-off run — no further repeat is authorized until the chef-owner reviews these results and decides.

On 2024-07-17, the chef-owner authorized a prep cook (already scheduled for the 2024-07-26 shift) to help Sam stage sheet pans for a new trial. Because the 60-min ceiling is a proxy for added labor cost (the original blocker was "three extra staff-hours"), the recommended logging method for this multi-person trial is: log only trial-specific task minutes per person (not the prep cook's regular scheduled duties), sum minutes across people rather than measuring wall-clock overlap, and compare that summed total against the unchanged 60-min ceiling — flagging to the chef-owner that this is the first multi-person version of the test vs. the solo-Sam June 28 baseline (57 min).

On 2024-07-24, the chef-owner moved that prep cook to another station, changing the Friday trial's staffing: Sam now handles seasoning and oven staging, and a line cook stages and clears pans between their existing duties (rather than a dedicated prep cook). Recommended task sequence: line cook stages raw pieces on pans → Sam seasons → Sam oven-stages → bake → line cook clears pans. Because staging/clearing (line cook) and seasoning/oven-staging (Sam) fall at different points in the sequence rather than overlapping, per-person task-specific stopwatch logging (not clock-in/out) naturally avoids double-counting; sum both people's logged minutes and compare against the unchanged 60-min ceiling, 44-portion yield floor, and the 57-min solo-Sam June 28 baseline — flagging this as a second, distinct multi-person configuration (Sam + line cook) vs. both the solo baseline and the 7-17-24 authorized Sam + prep-cook version.

On 2024-07-26, Sam ran the first scheduled repeat using the tested sequence: 59 incremental min (under the 60-min ceiling), 30lb raw case produced 44 complete portions (met the ≥44-portion floor). Of those, 40 sold at $18 each (revenue $720) and the remaining 4 were handled under the approved staff-meal procedure. Food cost $146, incremental labor $23.60 (at $24/hr), contribution = $550.40. Production is repeatable, but 40/44 sold is weaker sell-through than the 6-28-24 run (43/45 sold); the chef-owner still requires the 2024-08-16 repeat before deciding on any standing menu addition.

On 2024-08-08, Sam confirmed the supplier accepted the unchanged 30lb raw chicken case order before the 2:00pm deadline for the 2024-08-16 controlled repeat. No changes to test parameters: same pre-staging/tray sequence, 60-min incremental-labor ceiling, ≥44-portion yield floor, and sell-through/unsold-disposition logging. This is only the supply order confirmation — the repeat itself and the chef-owner's menu decision remain pending.

On 2024-08-16, Sam ran the second scheduled repeat using the unchanged 30lb case and tested pre-staging sequence: 56 incremental min (under the 60-min ceiling), yielding 45 complete portions (met the ≥44-portion floor). Of those, 44 sold at $18 each (revenue $792) and 1 was retained for staff meal. Food cost $146, incremental labor $22.40 (at $24/hr), contribution = $623.60. Sell-through was 44/45, stronger than the 7-26-24 repeat's 40/44. Across all three runs (6-28, 7-26, 8-16), production is repeatable within the labor/yield controls while demand varies by run; the chef-owner's decision on the dish's standing place was still pending after this run.

On 2024-08-19, the chef-owner reviewed all three sale-run records (6-28, 7-26, 8-16-24) and made the final call: production/labor thresholds were met every time, but sell-through varied enough (43/45 → 40/44 → 44/45) that the dish will not become a standing weekly special. Instead it's approved as an advance-count option for private dinners, so Sam can size the batch to a known guest count using the tested pre-staging sequence. This doesn't change Sam's head-chef role. This closes the thread — no further sale-run testing or menu-decision follow-up is open.

On 2024-09-13 (private dinner), the first real application of the 8-19-24 advance-count model: 32 chicken + 4 vegetarian meals confirmed, supplier case expected to yield 36 complete chicken portions after trim (4 more than the 32 confirmed chicken orders). Sam wanted the 4 extra treated as an internal service contingency for trim-yield variance, not as included/advertised refills, to avoid recreating an open-ended weekly-sale batch. Recommended treatment: hold as kitchen-side buffer only (not plated/announced to guests), and route any unused portions through the existing staff-meal disposition if trim comes in as expected — using the tested pre-staging/tray sequence, no new batch-plan test required.

Service outcome, reported by Sam late that night (2024-09-13, ~11:20pm): all 30 chicken-guests and 6 vegetarian-guests (36 total, final headcount split differed slightly from the 32/4 pre-service confirmation but total matched) received their confirmed meals. One plated chicken portion was lost to a dropped platter before service; the chef covered it by releasing one of the three contingency portions on hand. The remaining two contingency portions stayed in the kitchen and were not offered as seconds — matching the "internal buffer, not advertised refills" treatment agreed pre-service. No open-batch or recurring-menu promise was made. This closes out the first private-dinner application cleanly.

On 2024-09-14, Sam compiled the full operational numbers for the 9-13-24 dinner: actual case trim yielded 33 complete chicken portions (lower than the 36 projected pre-service), incremental chicken prep/handling totaled 51 min (under the 60-min ceiling). Reconciling categories: demand = 30 confirmed chicken orders (unchanged — the platter-drop replacement is a fulfillment substitution for an already-counted order, not added demand); of the 3 contingency portions (33 yield − 30 orders), 1 was consumed for the replacement and 2 went unused, routed to the standing staff-meal disposition rather than logged as unsold/failed sell-through (they were never held out for sale). This finalizes the 9-13-24 record — no new dinner or menu-status change.

On 2024-09-30, the host of a 2024-10-19 private dinner (28 adults) settled on 23 chicken + 5 vegetarian meals, confirmed against the supplier's guarantee of 25 complete chicken portions from one case. The 23 chicken orders are committed guest meals; the remaining 2 guaranteed portions are kitchen-only contingency, not advertised or offered as promised seconds — same internal-buffer treatment established 9-13-24. Sam will use the tested pre-staging sequence. This is another advance-count private-dinner booking under the 8-19-24 model, not a change to standing-menu status or Sam's role.

On 2024-10-08, the restaurant returned a corrected version of the 10-19-24 service sheet: 23 chicken + 5 vegetarian meals for the 28 adults, with the 2 additional guaranteed chicken portions explicitly labeled kitchen-only contingency (not seconds). The correction removed an earlier draft's promise that seconds may be served, while keeping the tested pre-staging sequence and not adding roasted chicken to the weekly menu. The service-sheet correction is complete — no further edits pending for this booking.

On 2024-10-19, the dinner was served: the single case yielded exactly 25 complete chicken portions as guaranteed. All 23 booked chicken meals and all 5 vegetarian meals were served. Both extra chicken portions stayed in the kitchen throughout service, were not offered as seconds, and were not counted as demand — matching the kitchen-only contingency treatment set in the 10-8-24 corrected service sheet. Incremental chicken prep/handling took 48 min, under the 60-min ceiling. This closes out the 10-19-24 booking cleanly — second successful application of the advance-count private-dinner model.

On 2024-10-21, Sam and the chef-owner reviewed the September and October private-dinner records (9-13-24 and 10-19-24) and formalized the advance-count model into a standing per-booking rule, in effect through the holiday season: a one-case booking may commit no more than 23 chicken meals, must preserve two kitchen-only contingency portions, and requires the final entrée split (chicken vs. vegetarian/other) locked seven days before service. The tested pre-staging/tray sequence remains the production method. The dish stays off the standing weekly menu, and this doesn't change Sam's head-chef role. This closes the standardization step — future private-dinner bookings should follow this rule directly rather than being treated as new one-off tests.

On 2025-09-21, Sam wrote up general principles for a culinary panel, generalizing lessons from this thread: advance counts align purchasing/prep with known demand; menu and production authority can be exercised without the approving chef attending every service (echoes [[project_sam_restaurant_offer_mar2025]]'s 5-12-25 finding that private-dining approval authority is separable from personal-attendance obligation); customization should be declined when it compromises allergen handling, the tested production sequence, or a realistic staffing commitment (echoes the 1-23/1-24-25 sesame-allergy resolution, which used a separate dedicated-pan plate rather than modifying the tested chicken recipe). The note reaffirms that roasted chicken remains an advance-count private-event option, not a weekly menu item — no change to the standing 10-21-24 rule.

**Why:** Narrows what's actually next for this thread — not a general "special did well" story, but a specific cost constraint (3hrs → ≤1hr) blocking any repeat, resolved into a bounded conditional sale-run approval that ran three times (6-28, 7-26, 8-16-24), consistently clearing the production/labor bar while sell-through fluctuated enough that the chef-owner settled on private-dinner advance-count use instead of a standing special (decided 8-19-24). The 9-13-24 dinner was the first live test of that advance-count model, and it held even with a dropped-platter loss — validates the contingency-buffer approach. The 10-19-24 booking (confirmed 9-30-24) is a second application of the same model, using the supplier's guarantee number as the contingency ceiling rather than a projected trim yield, and it also closed clean with the guaranteed yield hit exactly and contingency portions untouched.

**How to apply:** This thread is closed — don't ask about further sale-run tests or a pending standing-menu decision. The roasted-chicken dish is now a private-dinner, advance-count-only item (not a regular menu/special), sized to a known guest count using the tested pre-staging/tray sequence; Sam's role is unchanged. As of 10-21-24, treat this as a standing rule rather than a case-by-case negotiation: cap at 23 chicken meals per one-case booking, always hold back 2 kitchen-only contingency portions (never offered as guest seconds), and lock the final entrée split 7 days before service — in effect through the holiday season. Note the 23-cap is not automatically absolute: the 1-25-25 booking got a one-off event-specific production approval for 24 chicken (resolved 1-21-25), separate from and not a precedent for changing the standing cap — bookings that exceed the cap still need a fresh chef-owner decision, not an assumption that the exception carries forward. The Friday trial staffing was Sam (seasoning/oven staging) + a line cook (pan staging/clearing between other duties) as of 7-24-24 — still relevant if the pre-staging sequence comes up for private-dinner planning. The 1-25-25 booking's sesame-allergy issue is now closed (1-24-25): that guest moved to a dedicated-pan vegetarian plate, no sesame-free claim on the chicken, final split 23 chicken/7 vegetarian — don't treat this as an open safety item going forward. See [[user_hobbies_household]] for general Sam/restaurant context.

On 2025-01-11, a host inquiry for a January private dinner (30 guests) requested 24 chicken + 6 vegetarian meals, with a quote needed before the final split is due. This exceeds the 23-chicken one-case cap and falls outside the "through the holiday season" window the 10-21-24 rule was explicitly scoped to — so neither the cap nor the season-bound authorization automatically covers this booking. The 24-count is not yet approved; treat this as requiring a fresh chef-owner decision (on both the count and whether/how the rule extends past the holidays) before Sam quotes the host, rather than assuming the standing rule applies as-is.

Same day, assessed the yield math: one case has guaranteed 25 complete portions (per the 9-30-24 booking's supplier guarantee). 24 guest meals + the standard 2-portion kitchen-only contingency = 26, exceeding a single case's guaranteed yield by 1 — so covering 24 guests while preserving the usual 2-portion buffer would require either a second case/different batch plan or accepting only 1 contingency portion, both chef-owner decisions. Until the chef-owner rules on (a) whether 24 is approved at all, (b) how the yield shortfall is resolved, and (c) whether the standing rule extends past the holiday season into January, Sam should tell the host the headcount is noted but not quote a confirmed chicken count, price, or promise of seconds.

On 2025-01-21, the private-events desk confirmed the revised quote and the host's acceptance of 24 chicken + 6 vegetarian for the 2025-01-25 dinner. The event sheet documents this under an event-specific production approval (distinct from the 23-cap holiday-season standing rule) and does not list chicken as a weekly-menu item. This resolves the 1-11-25 open question: the chef-owner approved 24 chicken for this booking specifically, rather than extending or amending the 23-chicken standing cap. The dish remains off the standing weekly menu.

On 2025-01-23, the host flagged that one of the guests currently listed for chicken has a severe sesame allergy. Kitchen notes: the roasted-chicken sauce contains toasted sesame oil, and the standard garnish uses a shared sesame prep surface — both are direct/cross-contact risks as currently prepared. Vegetarian prep can be kept separate. The dinner is still confirmed at 24 chicken + 6 vegetarian pending resolution. Sam does not want the event desk to tell the host the chicken is sesame-free, and does not want the entrée split changed, until the chef-owner makes a safety/production call (e.g., sauce/garnish modification for that guest, a dedicated allergen-safe prep pass, or moving that guest to the vegetarian count). This is now the open item on the booking — not yet resolved.

On 2025-01-24, the chef-owner and event desk resolved the allergy question: the sesame-allergic guest was moved to a vegetarian plate prepared with a dedicated pan and utensils (rather than modifying the chicken sauce/garnish). No sesame-free claim is being made about the roasted chicken itself. This shifted the 1-25-25 dinner's final service split from 24/6 to 23 chicken + 7 vegetarian — which also brings the chicken count back within the standard 23-meal cap, though the shift happened for allergy-safety reasons, not to enforce the cap. This closes the sesame-allergy item cleanly.

On 2025-09-27, Sam brought home a written draft holiday private-dining policy for roasted chicken, formalizing the dish's status into policy language: it's an advance-count private-event option, not a weekly menu item; a one-case booking may commit no more than 23 guest portions while preserving two kitchen-only contingency portions; the final entrée split is due seven days before service; and Sam's menu/production approval does not itself assign him to service coverage. This is a draft, not yet confirmed as adopted — but every term matches the standing 10-21-24 rule and the 9-21-25 generalized principles exactly, including the service-coverage/approval separation that echoes the 5-12-25 finding in [[project_sam_restaurant_offer_mar2025]]. Treat this as the existing practice being written into formal policy, not a new negotiation or a change in terms.

On 2026-09-19, Sam received a proposed final entrée split for a 30-guest private dinner: 24 chicken + 6 vegetarian. This exceeds the standard 23-chicken one-case cap (same overage pattern as the 1-25-25 booking) and, on the guaranteed 25-portion-per-case yield used since 9-30-24, 24 guest meals + the usual 2-portion contingency = 26 — 1 over guaranteed yield. Not yet resolved: whether the chef-owner has approved 24 as an event-specific exception (as in 1-21-25) and how the 1-portion yield shortfall is handled (reduced contingency vs. second case/different batch plan).

Same day, Sam sent the host a response holding the booking at the standing cap (23 chicken + 7 vegetarian) rather than treating the 24-count request as pre-approved, since no chef-owner exception (like the 1-21-25 one) had been granted for this booking. The response reiterated the 2-portion kitchen-only contingency, the 7-day-out final-count deadline, and that roasted chicken is a private-event-only item, not a standing menu offering.

On 2027-07-24, Sam received a production sheet for a 48-guest private dinner: 34 chicken + 14 vegetarian confirmed guest meals (34+14=48, matching guest count), plus a 4-portion kitchen-only chicken contingency, for a chicken production total of 38 portions (34+4). This is larger in scale than any prior logged booking (previous largest was 30 guests) and both the 34-chicken guest count and the 4-portion contingency exceed the standing 10-21-24 per-one-case terms (23-chicken cap, 2-portion contingency) with no chef-owner exception noted on the sheet (unlike the 1-21-25 event-specific approval for the 1-25-25 24-count booking). Not yet resolved: whether this reflects a chef-owner-approved multi-case scaling of the standing rule, or needs a fresh exception/approval before service.

On 2025-02-01, Sam's test-dish worksheet for a new (non-chicken) dish showed: 20 portions, ingredients $8.10/portion ($162 total), direct labor 3.5 hrs at $28/hr ($98 total) — combined $260. Proposed menu price $26/portion ($520 revenue for the batch). Target is ingredient+labor ≤42% of menu revenue.

Actual ratio was $260/$520 = 50%, 8 points over the 42% target. On 2025-02-05, Sam took this costing back to the chef-owner, who declined to test the dish at the current $260 cost / $26 price since it exceeds 42%. The chef-owner will only reconsider a redesigned 20-portion version, and only if ingredients + direct labor come to ≤$218.40 at the same $26 price.

On 2025-02-08, Sam's redesigned 20-portion worksheet came in at: ingredients $7.20/portion ($144 total), direct labor 2.5 hrs at $28/hr ($70 total) — combined $214.00, under the $218.40 threshold (and ~41.2% of the $520 revenue at $26/portion, under the 42% target). This version meets the chef-owner's stated bar for reconsideration.

On 2025-02-13, the chef-owner approved one controlled 20-portion test of this redesigned braised dish at the unchanged $26 menu price, based on the documented $214 ingredient-and-direct-labor cost. This approval is limited to testing the redesigned preparation — it is not menu approval and does not authorize a recurring dish.

On 2025-02-21, the controlled test ran: 20 portions at $26, ingredients $143.40, direct labor 2.65 hrs at $28/hr ($74.20), for a combined $217.60 — under the $218.40 ceiling. All 20 portions were served, but prep finished 9 minutes past the station target, and 2 held portions showed slight sauce separation before service.

On 2025-02-24, the chef-owner reviewed the 2-21-25 test: the $217.60 cost was accepted as within ceiling, but the 9-minute station overrun and sauce separation in the 2 held portions blocked menu approval. name: project-watercolor-wet-edge-timing-test-aug2025
description: 8-9-25 wet-edge clinic test + 8-24-25, 8-31-25, 9-7-25 follow-ups — re-entry timing for cool street wash vs warm doorway edge, narrowed to 5.5-7 min window with 5.5 min feathering slightly
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: project
  originSessionId: 0e0451eb-6932-44db-8e75-c18d7317f1f1
  modified: 2026-09-19T01:52:12.928Z
---

At the wet-edge watercolor clinic on 2025-08-09, tested the same cool street wash with three different re-entry timings into the warm doorway edge:
- ~3 min re-entry: broke the large wash, pulled dark into the warm edge (bad)
- ~7 min wait: kept the cool shape continuous and preserved the warm edge (best result)
- Fully dry before adding the rain mark: mark sat too sharply on top (bad)

Instructor advised changing only one variable in the next study.

Follow-up on 2025-08-24: tested a ~5-min re-entry, holding pigment mix (blue+brown neutral), paper, brush load, and cool-wash continuity constant. Wash stayed more continuous than the 3-min attempt and the warm edge stayed clearer, but a small bloom formed where the dark mark entered the still-damp wash. This narrowed the workable window to somewhere between 5 and 7 minutes — 5 min alone is not yet clean.

Follow-up on 2025-08-31: tested a ~6-min re-entry, same constants held. Wash and warm edge held (no bloom), but the rain mark landed slightly too crisp (leaning dry). Combined with the 7-min result (best, no crispness noted), this narrows the workable window further to roughly between 6 and 7 minutes, not 5-7 — bloom risk is on the wetter/lower side, crispness risk on the drier/higher side.

Follow-up on 2025-09-07: tested a ~5.5-min re-entry, same constants held (paper, blue+brown mix, brush load, cool wash, warm-edge goal). At 5 min the interruption bloomed; at 6 min it read slightly too crisp. At 5.5 min the cool wash stayed continuous and the warm edge stayed clear, but the lower end of the rain mark feathered slightly — not a clean result, but closer to clean than 5 min.

**Why:** Builds directly on [[project_rainy_doorway_instructor_feedback_jul2025]] (cool wash uninterrupted, dry warm edge, scrap-test dark before adding rain interruption) — this test isolates timing as that one variable across four rounds.

**How to apply:** For future rainy-doorway studies, treat 7 minutes as the confirmed-clean re-entry point, 6 minutes as clean-but-too-crisp, 5.5 minutes as close-but-feathering-at-the-low-end, and 5 minutes as bloom-prone; the workable window is narrowing toward the upper half (5.5-7, likely converging near 6.5-7). Next recommended single-variable test is ~6.5 minutes to bisect the remaining 6-7 gap, holding pigment mix, paper, brush load, and cool-wash continuity constant. See also [[project_rainy_doorway_studies_inventory_jun2025]] and [[project_rainy_doorway_pigment_mix_tests_jul2025]].
